title: Santa Cruz County immigration arrests steadily increase as nationwide arrests surge
description:
At least four arrests this year Santa Cruz Local identified seven arrests in Santa Cruz County over the past two years in federal data.
Santa Cruz Local is requesting and compiling documentation of these “courtesy notices” in Santa Cruz County on an ongoing basis.
See notices provided to Santa Cruz Police, Watsonville Police, and the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office.
The Santa Cruz County Office of the Public Defender assists non-citizens who pled guilty or no-contest without fully understanding their sentence.
Nonprofits that provide immigration legal assistance include Santa Cruz County Immigration Project: Catholic Charities, Watsonville Law Center, and Latinan.
text:
At least four arrests this year

Santa Cruz Local identified seven arrests in Santa Cruz County over the past two years in federal data. Additional arrests may have occurred if federal agents did not clearly document their location. Numerous arrests in the data are missing location information.

Across Northern California, ICE has increasingly targeted people without a criminal record. But in Santa Cruz County, most documented arrests have been of people with charges or past convictions.

An ICE spokesman shared details about two recent cases but declined to elaborate on the details of all cases identified by Santa Cruz Local, or to confirm the total number of arrests in Santa Cruz County since 2025.

On Aug. 5, ICE agents arrested 29-year-old Mexican national Martin Sebastian Cruz Diaz in Watsonville, ICE spokesperson Jason Sweeney wrote in a Sept. 4 statement. After years in jail, he was convicted in February of numerous charges, including lewd and lascivious acts with a child aged 14 or 15, and released later that month on time served.

Three people arrested in the county had criminal convictions, and two had pending charges, according to the federal data. One person was documented as having violated only immigration law, and another as having outstanding charges in another country.

One of the two without a criminal record in the U.S. is 64-year-old Canadian national Charles Peter Billone, arrested July 29, who officials said had an arrest warrant in Canada for sexual assault and sexual contact with a child under 14.

One arrest on April 15, 2025, took place at the Santa Cruz County Jail as part of the Criminal Alien Program, a federal effort to arrest people in the country illegally as they leave jail or prison for other offenses.

Ashley Keene, a spokesperson for the Sheriff’s Office, wrote in an Aug. 31 email that their office had no knowledge of the arrest at the jail.

“We do not participate in nor do we coordinate with ICE regarding immigration enforcement actions,” she wrote. “ICE being able to take someone into custody at or near the jail does not mean our agency transferred the person to ICE or cooperated with ICE’s immigration enforcement.”

Phil Neff, lead analyst for the Deportation Data Project, confirmed in an email that not all arrests through the Criminal Alien Program involve collaboration with local law enforcement. This is in part because immigration officials can use jail information shared with the Federal Bureau of Investigation and publicly available jail and court records, to locate and arrest non-citizens leaving jails.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection, or CBP, can also arrest people for immigration-related charges. Increasingly, CBP has carried out arrests far from the borderlands. As border crossings dropped precipitously at the start of Trump’s second term, CBP, which includes border patrol, has had more capacity to conduct enforcement in the interior and to support ICE.

The CBP data obtained by the Deportation Data Project includes the date and time of those arrests, but not the location — meaning the agency may have also arrested people in Santa Cruz County.

An arrest reported by Lookout Santa Cruz alleged to have occurred on Jan. 18, 2025 was not identifiable in ICE, CBP or detention center data. A CBP spokesperson said there was no record of the arrest. Santa Cruz Local was not able to independently verify the arrest and did not include it in our data analysis.

Santa Cruz County Public Defender Heather Rodgers has called for more funding for immigration attorneys in her office to assist residents and expand the services it provides. (Amaya Edwards — Santa Cruz Local/CatchLight Local file)

Notifications to local law enforcement have slowed

Federal immigration agents often notify local law enforcement of their presence ahead of time. Santa Cruz Local is requesting and compiling documentation of these “courtesy notices” in Santa Cruz County on an ongoing basis.

Notices to local law enforcement have decreased since a high of five visits in January, with one visit a month reported in June, July and August. It’s unclear how many visits have been made without informing local law enforcement. For example, there is no record of federal authorities notifying Watsonville Police Department ahead of the Aug. 5 arrest.

See notices provided to Santa Cruz Police, Watsonville Police, and the Santa Cruz County Sheriff’s Office. Scotts Valley Police and Capitola Police reported no notices from federal immigration authorities in the past two years.

Arrests nationally and regionally are increasing

Across the San Francisco Area of Responsibility, which includes Northern California, Hawaii, Guam and the Saipan, arrests have sharply increased over the past six months.

The city with the most arrests since January 2025 — 2,481 — is San Francisco, where an immigration court has been the site of more than 140 courthouse arrests and more than 500 people were arrested during immigration appointments at an ICE field office. Some of those arrested could have been Santa Cruz County residents because San Francisco and Concord are the closest immigration courts.

Other cities with the most arrests include Fresno, Bakersfield, Sacramento and Stockton.

Officials are increasingly not taking people into detention after they are arrested, possibly a sign that other means, including ankle monitors, are being used to monitor arrestees awaiting a court date. That doesn’t appear to be the case for any of the documented arrests in Santa Cruz County.

And although nearly all the people arrested in Santa Cruz County had current or pending criminal charges, an increasing number of people in Northern California have been arrested with no criminal record.

Legal resources for immigrants

Some criminal sentences can bar non-citizens from pursuing legal status, or otherwise place them at a higher risk of deportation. Some people with these sentences may be able to retroactively remove the parts that impact immigration pathways.

The Santa Cruz County Office of the Public Defender assists non-citizens who pled guilty or no-contest without fully understanding their sentence. Often, people plead guilty, “not understanding that it was going to be devastating to their immigration pathways,” said Public Defender Heather Rodgers, “which in turn could impact their ability, especially in this administration, to stay with their families and to raise their children and continue on with their life in this country.”

Public defenders petition the District Attorney to remove or substitute immigration-related penalties. “We have a very high success rate on those petitions,” she said.

In some cases, the public defender’s office may be able to dismiss charges, expunge or seal criminal records, or obtain a vacatur that essentially erases the conviction.

There’s no guarantee that any of these measures will decrease someone’s likelihood of arrest or detention. “At times during this administration, things have felt a little arbitrary,” Rodgers said.

People with pending criminal charges should seek attorneys in both criminal and immigration court, Rodgers said. The Public Defender’s office represents those who cannot afford a private attorney in criminal court, but does not work in immigration court.

Nonprofits that provide immigration legal assistance include Santa Cruz County Immigration Project: Catholic Charities, Watsonville Law Center, and Latinan.

For a private immigration lawyer, Rodgers suggests relying on referrals from a trusted source, like nonprofit legal agencies or the Lawyer Referral Service of Santa Cruz County. Scams are common, especially on social media like Facebook. Notaries are not authorized to provide legal services.

Read more about immigrant rights, making an emergency plan for arrest and other resources.

title: A cartel tortured Julio: The US denied his family asylum and wants to send them to a third country
description:
“I can’t get out of here,” Blanca Hernández recalls her son saying, when he confessed that organized crime had recruited him.
“They want to send us to Ecuador, but it’s worse than Mexico,” says Alondra De Ávila, Julio’s younger sister.
She says Julio was forced to work for a cartel, and that there came a point when a hitman accompanied him everywhere.
Only a year ago, this family laments, the Jalisco State Attorney General’s Office issued its first missing person report for Julio.
But on April 13, 2026, the family received a devastating blow: an immigration judge granted the government’s request to close their asylum application and denied them protections against deportation.
text:
Julio thought that he had found his dream job. He was a driver for a wealthy family in Guadalajara, Mexico’s second-largest city.

At first, his tasks were simple: taking his employer to the beauty salon, shopping, or for tea with her friends. He dropped her children off at school and then took them to their English, piano and swimming lessons. But everything changed when he discovered that they were the wife and children of a drug trafficker. “I can’t get out of here,” Blanca Hernández recalls her son saying, when he confessed that organized crime had recruited him. “The boss has already started asking me to deliver packages,” he told her, horrified, back in 2016.

Ten years later, Julio Alfredo De Ávila Hernández is missing. And several of his relatives now live in the United States: they fled the state of Jalisco without imagining that, by seeking asylum, they would enter a legal labyrinth. Their case has become intertwined with the Trump administration’s harsh immigration policies, which mandate the transfer of asylum seekers to third countries deemed “safe.” This is in order to avoid forcing them to return to their countries of origin, where their lives would be in danger.

In April of 2026, an immigration judge presented options to Julio’s parents and siblings: they could continue their asylum process in Ecuador, Honduras, or Guatemala (in that order). They’ve since initiated an appeal process to try to remain in the United States. “They want to send us to Ecuador, but it’s worse than Mexico,” says Alondra De Ávila, Julio’s younger sister.

Back in 2024, she crossed the border with her son — now four years old — to surrender to immigration authorities and tell her story. “We want to stay here. I don’t want my son to experience what I went through,” the 26-year-old pleads.

Julio’s life in Mexico’s criminal underworld

The day Julio accepted the first package his boss handed him, he knew there would be more to come. When he refused to carry out one of the assignments, the threat was immediate. “He told me that, if I quit working for him, he would kill my family, my wife and my children,” recalls Blanca Hernández, 59, describing a conversation she had with her son.

She says Julio was forced to work for a cartel, and that there came a point when a hitman accompanied him everywhere. They knew where he lived, who his relatives were and what his daily routines looked like. By that point, Julio had no way out.

“He saw them making the cocaine bricks. At parties, my son said, instead of putting out bottles [of alcohol], they would put out a tray with just lines [of cocaine]. They started forcing him to do drugs. If he didn’t want to, they pulled out guns. My son started becoming addicted to drugs,” his mother recounts. “He told me that he had stopped visiting us for our own good, so as not to involve us in his life.”

Blanca’s fears came to pass in the early hours of April 5, 2017. Julio was 31 at the time. A phone call alerted her that something had happened at her son’s home in Tlajomulco de Zúñiga, 20 miles south of Guadalajara. When she arrived, she found a heartbreaking scene. “There were pieces of flesh, already dried. I believe they were my son’s. There was a lot of blood in both bedrooms and in the kitchen. I had never seen so much blood,” she recounts.

Some witnesses told her that, hours earlier, armed men had arrived, wearing what appeared to be police badges. They were traveling in two pickup trucks. “They took out a person [from the house], wrapped in a blanket. It looked like a dead body. They threw him in the truck. Then, they took out a woman and, finally, my son, covered in blood, semi-conscious,” she says.

The family sprang into action. They filed a complaint with the Jalisco Attorney General’s Office, called everyone they knew, plastered Julio’s photograph around the city, spoke to the media and even offered a reward for information that might help locate him. But their efforts had an unexpected consequence: they angered the cartel. Vehicles carrying hooded men armed with assault rifles began following them. Then came direct threats, first through anonymous phone calls.

“They told me that they were the ones who had taken Julio and that they wanted me to hand over what Julio owed them,” reads the statement that Blanca Hernández gave to the Jalisco State Police’s Investigative Division. “If I didn’t, they said that they would cut off my head,” she continues.

Two weeks after Julio’s disappearance, one of his sisters received a video call: she saw her brother being tortured.

“He was covered in blood. They had him tied up. They pulled his hair to lift up his head. My son was covered in bruises. His face was swollen from the punches and covered in blood. His white tank top was completely red with blood,” his mother describes.

That was the last time the family saw him alive. Some time later, a video began circulating on El Blog del Narco, a website that publishes uncensored content related to organized crime in Mexico, showing a horrific act. This is how Jéssica, Julio’s younger sister, describes it: “They were cutting off his hand, from the wrist down. The police in Mexico showed us that video.” The family was able to identify him by a tattoo with his daughter’s name on one of his forearms.

Persecution in Mexico

The cartel made it clear that its threats were serious when several gunmen showed up at the family’s home. They pounded on the door and demanded that Julio’s mother hand over “what Julio had left behind,” according to her statement to investigators. “I couldn’t even speak; I was so scared,” she recounted.

The harassment soon spread to their workplaces and the streets of their neighborhood. One afternoon, the gunmen did not even hesitate to approach two of Julio’s sisters as they were accompanied by small children. “We grabbed the baby from the stroller and ran,” Alondra De Ávila recalls. “When we got home, we locked everything up. We put the sofas in the doorways.”

As soon as they had the chance, they fled to the Guadalajara airport, considering it to be the safest place in the city. Thus began a long journey, passing through the homes of relatives in the states of Jalisco, Aguascalientes and Baja California.

Blanca Hernández lost all hope of finding her son alive the day she spoke with someone connected to drug trafficking. “He told me, ‘Please, ma’am, don’t look for him anymore. You’re in grave danger. They’re going to kill you all.’”

Officially, Julio is one of the approximately 135,000 missing persons in Mexico, a crisis that has reached record numbers in recent years (with organized crime playing a central role). Only a year ago, this family laments, the Jalisco State Attorney General’s Office issued its first missing person report for Julio. “My brother became just another missing person, but for us, he will always be our family member,” Jessica says.

“It’s all been very hard”

The family fled to Tijuana, but even there, they didn’t feel safe. In 2024, they decided to cross into the United States to surrender to the Border Patrol. They all passed the first hurdle in their asylum application: the credible fear interview. Afterward, they remained in immigration custody — some for days, others for months — until they were released and able to reach their destination.

The process continued. They began to get settled in the United States, like so many other migrants. They attended hearings, confident that they had enough evidence to win their case. They even had copies of the complaints they had filed in Mexico. But on April 13, 2026, the family received a devastating blow: an immigration judge granted the government’s request to close their asylum application and denied them protections against deportation. She ordered that they be sent to Ecuador or, failing that, to Honduras. Guatemala was left as a third option.

These three nations have cooperation agreements with the Trump administration, functioning as “safe third countries,” meaning they receive migrants and process their asylum claims there. Human rights and immigrant advocacy groups, however, have questioned whether they genuinely meet the protection standards required under U.S. law. The agreements were initially signed during Trump’s first term, but were suspended during Joe Biden’s presidency. Trump reactivated them after returning to the White House. In the case of Ecuador, the agreement came back into force in July, 2025.

“It’s all been very hard,” Blanca Hernández laments. “I told the judge that we were in grave danger in Mexico, but that, between going to Ecuador or returning to Mexico, I’d rather die in Mexico.” She adds: “It’s not right that, just because of a mistake my eldest son made, more people are going to die. I am asking the U.S. government to give us a chance. We’re not bad people. We didn’t come here to steal. We didn’t come here to take anything from you.”

Her daughter, Alondra De Ávila, agrees that, if they’re deported to their home country, “we would have to live in hiding; there’s nowhere safe for us there.”

Their appeal against the immigration judge’s ruling has given them a glimmer of hope. The family is determined to pursue the legal fight through every possible level of appeal. “My family isn’t asking for money. We just want to be allowed to stay in this country,” Jessica insists. “It’s unjust to deny us that protection.”

text:
The WMUR debate between U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, D-NH and Dr. Karishma Manzur Friday night for the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate included immigration reform, supporting Israel, and funding for police departments in New Hampshire.

Manzur is a medical scientist with a Ph.D. in biochemistry and molecular biology, and has spent over 20 years working on treatments for illnesses like epilepsy and depression. She also serves on the board of NH Ranked Choice Voting and previously served on the boards of NH Open Democracy Action and NH Peace Action, per her campaign website.

Pappas served three terms on New Hampshire’s Executive Council, where he fought to expand Medicaid, invest in renewable energy, and protect funding for Planned Parenthood. In Congress, he worked on several key issues per his website: pushing tax cuts for working families and small businesses; cracking down on predatory companies that target veterans and pollute our water; and standing up to Big Pharma to lower drug costs.

There were no Republican debates for the seat because former Senator John Sununu declined to participate.

Commentator Steve Bottari noted childcare costs nationwide are rising faster than inflation, and asked the candidates what their plan was to help reduce those costs.

Pappas said he’s been fighting to get resources to childcare providers so that they can open more slots, improve wages, and that they can “meet the needs of New Hampshire families.”

He also noted in the past he supported legislation that would cap childcare costs at seven percent of a family’s income and “ensure that we’re investing in our great providers in the state of New Hampshire.”

Manzur said: “It’s a very simple answer: universal childcare. We need that immediately. We’re already used to having from K-12 (Kindergarten through 12th grade), we should just expand it and allow children as young as six months to be a part of the public education program. This is going to alleviate all of the issues that families are facing.

“I am a mother, I have two children, and I also had to make these decisions: do I go to work, or do I stay home? Because childcare was so expensive, and this was already 20 years ago.”

Manzur added that the government is spending money on endless wars and suggested using some of those funds to invest in New Hampshire communities and its children.

Commentators pointed out that Pappas had been a “major supporter of the U.S.-Israel alliance,” and said many young Democrats say they’ll never vote for a candidate that supports Israel in any way. Pappas was asked if he would ever fully agree with the voters who want 100% opposition to Israel.

“I appreciate the passionate views on all sides, and we’ve got to be listening, and making sure that young people in particular have a voice… I think what’s important is that both Israelis and Palestinians have security and an opportunity to live in peace (and) coexist side-by-side.

“I support a two-state solution, I support increasing aid to the Palestinians right now, and making sure that this very fragile ceasefire gets to the next stages, so that the Israeli military will pull out of Gaza, Hamas will lay down their arms, and there’s an opportunity for civil society to be rebuilt,” Pappas said.

Bottari asked Manzur why she believed Israel was wrong to respond militarily to the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks by Hamas.

Manzur wanted to be clear that it wasn’t about Jewish people or their religion, but that it was about “Benjamin Netanyahu and his ultra right-wing government.”

Manzur said that Netanyahu has control over almost 90% of Congress as well as the White House. She said he’s addicted to killing, and that using “our troops, our money, and our weapons to advance his policies.”

“We must have a foreign policy based on national security and national interests, not the whims of a foreign genocidal government. We must bring the power back to the American people,” she said.

Commentators asked Manzur who they think should enforce immigration laws if Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) were to be abolished.

Manzur said she initially entered the country as an immigrant and went through the Immigration Naturalization Service under the Department of Justice, and never felt threatened or mistreated. She wants to return immigration efforts to a process like that, noting that there can still be immigration enforcement if ICE is abolished.

She said Pappas supported the Laken Riley Act which “empowered ICE to terrorize our communities.”

“The fact is, I’m standing up to (President) Donald Trump on immigration because it’s unacceptable what’s happening in the streets of America. With respect to that bill, that was about making sure immigrants that were undocumented and committing violent crimes are held accountable. I support — and I think the people of New Hampshire support — going after criminals who are committing violence in our communities.

“But we have got to make sure that we’re treating immigrants with dignity… People have been killed from Biddeford, Maine, to Texas and Minnesota, and it’s unacceptable,” Pappas responded.

Pappas was asked to specify how he would reform ICE, and said he’s led legislation to go after the “$75 billion slush fund they (the Trump Administration) were given in the big ugly bill (the Big Beautiful Bill) last year,” and wants to invest it in community-based policing.

Commentator Christa Delcamp said the U.S. Department of Justice sent more than $12 million to New Hampshire in 2025 to support local law enforcement. She said it provided money for training, equipment, and helped to hire personnel.

She asked both candidates if they thought that amount of spending should be increased, decreased, or eliminated.

Pappas said he thinks we should increase federal spending with respect to public safety “because it helps our local budgets,” and said he’s worked with different police chiefs to get modern radio and better equipment.

Manzur said her brother is a law enforcement officer in Indiana, and that she will always turn to law enforcement officials to understand their needs “and I will always address their needs, whatever it is they need.”

text:
Seven faith leaders were arrested in Williston, Vermont, on Sept. 4, charged with blockading the entrances to a building where workers help immigration agents target their efforts, with the clergy insisting their faith compels them to oppose President Donald Trump's ongoing mass deportation campaign.

The arrests occurred as faith leaders sought to decry the actions of the National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, one of three major facilities that help Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents hone their operations.

According to the Rev. Rebecca Girrell, a United Methodist pastor who took part in the protest and was among those arrested, faith leaders began blocking the building's entrances about 7:30 a.m. They remained there for roughly three hours, with the clergy singing, praying and reading the names of people Girrell said have "been killed in ICE interactions or died in detention."

Ultimately, Girrell was arrested by Vermont state police alongside six others: two United Church of Christ ministers, an Episcopal priest and the archdeacon of the Episcopal Diocese of Vermont, a Quaker leader and a Unitarian Universalist minister.

"I think it is imperative on me, as a faith leader, to proclaim that human beings are not targets and that God is a God of justice and of love," said Girrell, who serves United Community Church in Morrisville, Vermont, a congregation affiliated with both the UMC and the United Church of Christ.

"We are called to love our neighbors, to love the strangers and the foreigners that live among us, to recognize that we are all sojourners," she said.

According to footage recorded at the scene, at least two of the clergy were physically carried out of the center by law enforcement as they were arrested, including the Rev. Karen Johnston, senior minister at First Unitarian Universalist Society of Burlington. In a statement to Religion News Service, Johnston said she "refused to cooperate" with law enforcement, explaining that her UU values of "justice, equity, generosity, interdependence and transformation call (her) and all people of conscience and faith to actively not cooperate with the system of cruelty that is fueled by this center."

Later Sept. 4, Vermont State Police published mug shots of the faith leaders alongside a press release stating those arrested were charged with "unlawful trespass."

Representatives for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the protest.

The targeting center has been the site of multiple protests in recent months, organized by what Girrell described as a "loose consortium of concerned neighbors." Advocates have focused their efforts on the targeting center, she said, because of the significant role it plays in directing ICE's actions elsewhere in the country.

The pastor added that while this is her first time being arrested at the building — which is private property, not a federal facility, and includes offices of other groups that are not tied to ICE — she had attended three similar protests there. But past protests were not led by faith leaders, Girrell said, and she believes it's important to showcase religious resistance to an administration that has often invoked faith while pursuing its policy goals.

"Christianity, especially, gets painted into a very pro-government, pro-deportation, Christian nationalist flavor," she said. "It's so important to realize that's a loud voice, but I don't even think it's the most prevalent voice."

The arrests add to a growing list of clergy who have encountered law enforcement while protesting against the Trump administration's immigration policies. Last fall, at least seven faith leaders were arrested while protesting outside an ICE facility in Broadview, Illinois, where clergy said they had previously been shot with pepper balls fired by federal agents while protesting in the area. In January, about 100 clergy were also arrested while staging a protest outside the Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport, with faith leaders occupying the busy street in front of the facility to speak out against ICE activity there that had resulted in the detention of some workers.

Dozens of individual faith leaders, religious groups and entire denominations have also filed at least 22 lawsuits challenging Trump's immigration policies since he was inaugurated, and hundreds of other faith leaders across the country have been trained to observe and resist the ICE efforts.

Girrell said she met some of the clergy arrested Sept. 4 at one such training that took place in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in January. The Methodist pastor, who spoke to RNS at the time, was one of more than 600 clergy who flew to the city to help push back against the thousands of immigration agents who had descended on the region.

The Sept. 4 protest in Williston, she said, is part of her effort to draw on what she learned at that gathering and push back against ICE in her own state.

"We really wanted to make a statement, as people of faith and conscience, about how we need to be responding and showing up in the face of this injustice and dehumanization in Vermont," Girrell said.

text:
Humberto Castro, a 59-year-old Venezuelan, was driving to work as usual from his home in Doral, where he has lived for eight years, when he was detained by agents from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“My dad has a work permit valid until 2030. His asylum case is pending. He was on his way to work, driving normally, and they pulled him over and handcuffed him,” said his daughter, Arianna Castro, 29. Her father arrived in the U.S. on a visa and has an asylum application pending, she said. He has no criminal record.

Castro’s case comes amid a wave of immigrant arrests in South Florida that has alarmed the Venezuelan community, which is the largest in the United States. Now, with just three months to go before the midterm elections, they are demanding answers and concrete measures from their congressional representatives.

Two leading exile organizations, Venezuelans Persecuted for Political Reasons in Exile (Veppex) and the multicultural activists group Voice and Expression (Amavex), have prepared a report they sent to members of Congress asking for an investigation into the detentions of Venezuelans with pending asylum claims and other immigration cases.

The report says that Venezuelans in the United States have been affected by the rollback of temporary and humanitarian protections, and that people with pending asylum claims and other immigration cases are being detained for deportation, including to distant third countries such as Liberia. It also notes that the authorities do not publish data on how many detained Venezuelans have criminal records or pending immigration proceedings.

As a point of reference, the report notes that as of July, about 65,765 people were in ICE custody, more than 70% of whom had no criminal record. It also documents at least three cases of Venezuelans detained between July and August despite having work authorization and pending asylum claims.

Helen Villalonga, president of Amavex, says the Trump administration’s immigration policies have “brutally harmed” the community.

Nearly half the population of Doral, a city in Miami-Dade County, is Venezuelan. Last year, the city entered into a 287(g) agreement to cooperate with federal immigration authorities.

Much of South Florida’s Venezuelan community supported Donald Trump in the last election, expecting that he would increase pressure on Nicolás Maduro’s regime in Venezuela and that the mass deportation campaign he promised would target criminals and people with ties to Chavismo, Villalonga says. Now, she adds, even Venezuelans with links to the Republican Party have called her after the report’s publication to say: “This isn’t what we voted for. This isn’t what we were expecting.”

Villalonga says the report is intended to put pressure on South Florida lawmakers ahead of the November elections. While some legislators have expressed sympathy for the plight of Venezuelans, she argues that this has yet to translate into meaningful solutions, and the report calls for concrete results. According to Villalonga, none of the lawmakers have acknowledged receiving the document since it was sent to them.

“We are tired of [lawmakers] issuing statements on social media or sending a letter. What we need are immediate actions in Congress, actions within the Department of Homeland Security, within the State Department,” she said.

The report calls on Congress to hold oversight hearings on the detention of Venezuelans and to require DHS and ICE to publish data on detainees’ nationalities, criminal records and pending immigration cases. It also calls for a Government Accountability Office (GAO) audit of arrests carried out at airports. In addition, it urges DHS and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to review cases individually and pursue alternatives to detention for people with no criminal record who are complying with their immigration proceedings.

“It seems the administration has done the opposite of everything we have been asking for,” said José Antonio Colina, president of Veppex. “We agree that the government should enforce U.S. immigration laws, which seems reasonable. What we do not agree with is trying to criminalize Venezuelan immigration.”

The administration has taken actions that have left many people without legal status, Colina says. “Many who applied for political asylum are now being detained because that is not a status.”

In his view, lawmakers “have to move from rhetoric to action, because the facts and the actions show they have been neither forceful nor consistent.”

“I personally believe they [South Florida lawmakers] have no influence within the White House at the moment. They are not being heard,” he said. Representatives María Elvira Salazar, Carlos Giménez and Mario Díaz‑Balart, all Republicans, did not respond to requests for comment for this report. DHS did not respond either.

Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Wasserman Schultz told EL PAÍS that she is “deeply concerned by ICE’s recent push to arrest Venezuelans, Haitians and other law‑abiding immigrants at airports” and that she has contacted DHS about several issues related to ICE, “including the increase in its operations at airports and in our communities,” but so far has not received a concrete response.

Wasserman Schultz’s office added that several reports “have shown an increase in ICE activity at airports, and not only against Venezuelans.”

However, it noted that for the GAO to open an investigation, the request must come from “senior congressional leaders or the chairs or ranking minority members of committees or subcommittees with jurisdiction” over the issue. “Otherwise, requests are often rejected or go unanswered. The congresswoman does not fall into any of those categories when it comes to ICE oversight, but she is exploring the options available to her to push for an investigation and stronger oversight,” it said.

The issue puts the spotlight on two Miami lawmakers with oversight roles in Congress: Giménez, who chairs the Homeland Security subcommittee responsible for airport security, and Salazar, who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on the Western Hemisphere, which has jurisdiction over relations with Latin America.

Since January of last year, at the start of Trump’s second term, then Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem revoked Temporary Protected Status (TPS) protections for Venezuelans that the Biden administration had extended through October 2026, as well as humanitarian programs. DHS later terminated the 2021 and 2023 TPS designations.

More recently, the anti‑immigrant offensive has expanded to people with pending asylum cases who had been allowed to hold work permits. ICE agents are now detaining people whose asylum claims remain pending but whose visas have expired. DHS has also allowed certain asylum cases to be referred directly to immigration courts without an interview with USCIS.

Last year, the three Republican lawmakers from South Florida called for Venezuelans with no criminal record who had fled persecution under Maduro to be treated differently, and pledged to “do everything possible” to protect them. In January, Giménez urged Noem to adopt a “case-by-case solution” for exiles, while Salazar backed bipartisan legislation to grant TPS protections to “law-abiding” Venezuelans. In March, Salazar again called for protections for Venezuelans.

Maduro was captured in January in a U.S. military operation and is being held in New York awaiting trial. His vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, is acting as interim leader. The U.S. and Venezuela restored diplomatic relations in March, and last Friday, President Trump announced an agreement under which the United States will take control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves, more than double U.S. reserves.

Meanwhile, Arianna Castro says her father is being held at ICE offices in Miramar, north of Miami, and she is trying to secure his release on bond. “It feels totally unreal. We came here seeking a better life and all we have done is work, build a life here and contribute to the community,” she said. “My sister graduated from college; I also graduated; I’m a nurse. Now my husband doesn’t want me to leave the house. It’s strange to return to that fear we once had in Venezuela, that we couldn’t go out because we would be persecuted. You can’t live like that.”

text:
Mavis Belisle protested President Ronald Reagan’s policies outside the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas. Forty-two years later, she is preparing to return to the streets, this time to protest President Donald Trump.

Next week, Trump and Republicans will gather at the American Airlines Center for the party’s first midterm convention. Demonstrators plan to challenge his administration and its policies, much as they did in when Reagan accepted the GOP's nomination for a second term.

“The America that I grew up in hardly exists anymore, but it doesn’t make me want to give up,” Belisle said. “I’m ready to be back out there next week.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The issues that brought protesters to Dallas in 1984 included Reagan’s military buildup and policies in Central America, poverty, unemployment, homelessness, corporate power, government contracting and gay rights.

This year’s demonstrators are organizing around immigration, war, civil rights, economic hardship and concentrated political power.

The language and targets have changed. But the question of whether government is serving ordinary people has not.

A lifetime of organizing

Belisle, 82, an Oak Cliff resident, has spent decades protesting.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

She helped lead one of the largest acts of civil disobedience in Texas history at the Comanche Peak nuclear plant near Glen Rose. She later became executive director of the Peace Farm, a nonprofit focused on nuclear weapons and hazardous waste.

In 1984, she recruited and trained demonstrators as a member of the Dallas March and Rally Committee.

She rallied against Reagan’s military policies and the defense budget, which she believed contributed to poverty and economic inequality.

Organizers worked out of a small office on Ervay Street, not far from the city convention center. The cramped space became a hub for organizing peacekeepers.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“By being present at the same time and place that the Republican Party was, we could show those alternatives,” Belisle said.

She spent long, hot days that August moving between rallies, marches and a nearby tent city.

The encampment had little shade, inadequate water and only temporary toilets. At one point, Belisle was told to return to the organization’s office when police started arresting demonstrators. She spent the day making phone calls to raise bail money.

Familiar struggles

This year’s protest takes place during a midterm election cycle shaped by social media, national coalitions and concerns about immigration enforcement.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

But many of today’s grievances are familiar to Belisle.

Today’s organizers want to lower housing and food costs, stop aggressive immigration enforcement and hold the government accountable.

Like in 1984, protesters are bringing an anti-war message to the Republican convention.

Money spent on U.S. military action abroad, including in Iran, Israel and Palestine, comes at the expense of people struggling at home, said 35-year-old Jo Hargis, who is a member of the DFW Anti-War Committee.

Similar to Belisle decades earlier, Hargis has organized protests outside a Garland munitions plant and opposed partnerships linking the facility with local schools and colleges.

Article continues below this ad

The government must be pressured before it responds to ordinary people, Hargis said.

“We have power when we come together and exert our will,” Hargis said.

War, civil rights

In 1984, the Association of Community Organizations for Reform, or ACORN, held a national convention and created “Reagan Ranch,” a tent city near the Republican gathering to highlight poverty, homelessness and the experiences of low-income communities.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The Yippies organized more confrontational actions, while peace activists, gay-rights groups, anti-nuclear organizers and others opposed Reagan’s military buildup, policies in Central America and corporate power. About 1,500 people representing different causes marched during the convention.

The protests included marches, rallies and “die-ins” outside corporate buildings.

The most visible confrontation came Aug. 22, when Gregory Lee Johnson burned an American flag outside City Hall. Police arrested Johnson and dozens of other demonstrators. His conviction eventually reached the U.S. Supreme Court, which ruled in 1989 that flag burning was protected political speech.

One issue at a time

Belisle doesn’t regret taking part in the 1984 protests, which she said were largely peaceful, despite the tension and some arrests. She recalls only one serious injury .

She continues to encourage people to register to vote and participates in peace events and other organizing efforts. She said cooperation across liberal movements depends on people recognizing, honoring and working together.

Belisle knows this year’s march may not change the government immediately.

“You can change things, if not a whole lot, at least a little bit better, in little pieces at a time,” Belisle said.

text:
GILROY, Calif. (KGO) -- A federal judge in San Jose is scheduled to consider a preliminary injunction next week that could halt plans for a proposed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in Gilroy.

The project calls for construction on a 24-acre site east of the Gilroy Premium Outlets.

The proposal has faced opposition since plans were discovered in May, with critics arguing the facility would have negative effects on the community, including local schools.

Educators from across the South Bay are urging officials to stop the project, which would be located near the Gilroy Unified School District office.

"Student safety is not political. This is about every child's right to learn safely," said Santa Clara County Board of Education Trustee Maimona Afzal Berta.

MORE: ICE arrests in San Francisco Bay Area area up nearly 70%, data shows

"And this facility may be in Gilroy, but the fear doesn't stop at city limits," said Palo Alto Unified School District Board President Shounak Dharap.

Tuyen Fiack, president of the Gilroy Unified School District board, said more than half of students in Santa Clara County classrooms live in mixed-immigration-status households. She said those families could be harmed if the detention facility is built.

"When a child worries about whether their parent will be home when they return from school, that fear enters the classroom with them. And when children begin to associate the community where they live with fear rather than safety, we have an obligation to pay attention," Fiack said.

Opponents pointed to a recent case in nearby Morgan Hill involving the deportation of a father of three students in the Morgan Hill Unified School District.

Superintendent Carmen Garcia said such situations can have lasting effects on students.

MORE: ICE plans to purchase robot dogs

"Their trust in public institutions will be decimated because of the country they call home, betrayed their family and destroyed their American dream," Garcia said.

Santa Clara County Supervisor Sylvia Arenas, whose district includes the proposed site, said the project violates environmental and immigration laws. She said she intends to continue opposing the plans.

"It's not enough to have a campaign, and it's not enough to us to recognize a bill of rights for children. We have to make sure that we ring the alarm and that we organize," Arenas said.

Multiple Bay Area counties and the California attorney general have filed a lawsuit seeking to stop construction of the detention center. According to Attorney General Rob Bonta's office, the project remains paused until at least Sept. 9, a day after a federal judge is expected to consider the preliminary injunction.

On Friday, the federal judge presiding over the case signaled they may block construction of the ICE facility site.

Another hearing on the case is set for Tuesday.

Declaratory judgment vs quiet title: Declaratory judgment declares parties’ rights (e.g., what a deed conveyed).
text:
Supreme Court of Idaho (Sept. 4, 2026)

1. Introduction

Byrd v. Coffey is the Idaho Supreme Court’s second encounter with a dispute over littoral rights on Priest Lake. After an earlier administrative appeal concluded that the Idaho Department of Lands lacked authority to adjudicate competing littoral ownership in the first instance, the parties proceeded in district court via consolidated quiet title and declaratory judgment actions.

Parties. Stephan and Amy Byrd, and Erika Lynn Mullins and Allison Lindsey Still as co-trustees of the McCray Living Trust (collectively, “Byrds/Trust”), sought declarations and quiet title relief establishing that their parcels extended to the ordinary high water mark (OHWM) of Priest Lake (and thus carried littoral rights). Steven and Susan Coffey (“Coffeys”) counterclaimed for a contrary declaration, quiet title, and asserted civil trespass based on the Byrds/Trust’s dock and access across the disputed strip.

Core issue. The litigation turned on whether an older deed (Taylor-to-Tanner, the Byrds/Trust predecessor) conveyed title to the lake’s edge. The deed’s metes-and-bounds description referenced iron pins “on the shore of Priest Lake” and calls “along the shore.” The district court found the deed ambiguous, resorted to extrinsic evidence, and ultimately quieted title to a lakefront strip in the Coffeys, awarding trespass damages and fees.

Key appellate holding. The Supreme Court reversed—not because it definitively resolved the boundary—but because the district court applied the wrong burden of proof to the parties’ competing declaratory judgment claims interpreting an ambiguous deed.

2. Summary of the Opinion

New/clarified rule: When competing parties seek a declaratory judgment to interpret an ambiguous deed and determine who owns disputed land, the fact-finding question of the grantor’s intent is decided under the preponderance of the evidence standard. The clear and convincing standard applicable to certain quiet title theories does not govern the antecedent declaratory determination of ownership where title has not yet been declared in either party.

The Court affirmed the district court’s threshold legal conclusion that the Taylor-to-Tanner deed was ambiguous because “shore” had two reasonable interpretations. However, it held the district court erred by weighing the extrinsic evidence under a clear and convincing evidence standard for the parties’ declaratory judgment claims. The Court reversed, vacated the judgment (including trespass damages and attorney fees that flowed from the boundary determination), and remanded for the district court to reweigh the evidence using the preponderance standard (with discretion to rely on the existing record or conduct further proceedings).

3. Analysis

3.1 Precedents Cited

The Court’s reasoning is built on two clusters of authority: (i) doctrines governing littoral rights and navigable waters, and (ii) doctrines governing deed interpretation, burdens of proof, and appellate review.

A. Littoral rights and navigable waters

Byrd v. Idaho State Bd. of Land Comm'rs, 169 Idaho 922, 505 P.3d 708 (2022): This prior “first appeal” framed the dispute. It held IDL could not adjudicate littoral ownership in the first instance and signaled that a quiet title action was the appropriate vehicle. The 2026 Court relies on it to explain why ownership of the upland strip is inseparable from the littoral-rights question and why declaratory relief is central to resolving that ownership.

Newton v. MJK/BJK, LLC, 167 Idaho 236, 469 P.3d 23 (2020): Cited for the proposition that a littoral owner’s rights of access and use depend on adjacency to the navigable lake. It supplies the doctrinal bridge between boundary location and lake-use rights.

Lovitt v. Robideaux, 139 Idaho 322, 78 P.3d 389 (2003): Reinforces adjacency-based littoral rights and supports the Court’s summary of Idaho’s littoral framework.

Lake CDA Invs., LLC v. Idaho Dep't of Lands, 149 Idaho 274, 233 P.3d 721 (2010) and Erickson v. State, 132 Idaho 208, 970 P.2d 1 (1998): Cited for the equal-footing/statehood principle: the State owns the beds of navigable waters up to the high water mark, while littoral owners hold title down to the high water mark as it existed at statehood. These cases underscore why pin placement versus OHWM matters so much: a small strip can control access rights and lakebed interface.

I.C. § 58-1302(f): Statutory reinforcement of the littoral concept under Idaho’s lake protection framework.

B. Standards of review and deed interpretation framework

Chester v. Wild Idaho Adventures RV Park, LLC, 171 Idaho 212, 519 P.3d 1152 (2022): Supplies the bench-trial appellate template: substantial evidence review for fact findings; legal sufficiency review for conclusions of law.

C & G, Inc. v. Rule, 135 Idaho 763, 25 P.3d 76 (2001): Central to the Court’s bifurcated approach: ambiguity is a question of law (free review), while interpretation of an ambiguous instrument is a question of fact (deference if supported by substantial evidence). The Court uses it both to uphold the ambiguity finding and to define what must happen on remand (proper fact-finding under the correct burden).

Latvala v. Green Enters., Inc., 168 Idaho 686, 485 P.3d 1129 (2021): Provides the “substantial and competent evidence” definition, reinforcing that factual interpretation of ambiguity is ordinarily a trial-court function.

Baker v. KAL, LLC, 163 Idaho 530, 415 P.3d 939 (2018) and Camp Easton Forever, Inc. v. Inland Nw. Council Boy Scouts of Am., 156 Idaho 893, 332 P.3d 805 (2014): Used to articulate what makes language ambiguous and the requirement to read a deed as a whole.

Nielson v. Talbot, 163 Idaho 480, 415 P.3d 348 (2018): Referenced regarding “rules of construction” (e.g., prioritizing certain calls/monuments) as tools that apply once ambiguity exists; it supports the Court’s refusal to treat those rules as making the deed unambiguous on its face.

C. Burdens of proof: declaratory judgment vs quiet title

Luce v. Marble, 142 Idaho 264 (2005): The district court relied on this case for the proposition that a party claiming ownership where record title stands in another must prove its claim by clear and convincing evidence. The Supreme Court does not reject that rule; instead it holds it was prematurely applied to the declaratory judgment stage before the deed ambiguity and chain of title were resolved.

Watkins v. Fed. Life Ins. Co., 54 Idaho 174, 29 P.2d 1007 (1934): Cited for the baseline rule that factual issues in civil cases are determined by the preponderance of the evidence, anchoring the Court’s burden-of-proof correction.

Bear Crest Ltd. LLC v. State ex rel. Idaho Transp. Dep't, 176 Idaho 262, 575 P.3d 846 (2025): Cited for the proposition that deed interpretation follows contract interpretation principles, supporting the Court’s use of contract-burden and interpretive methodology by analogy.

A&B Irrigation Dist. v. Idaho Dep't of Water Res., 153 Idaho 500, 284 P.3d 225 (2012): Cited for applying preponderance to contract interpretation, reinforcing that the deed-intent fact question should be evaluated under the ordinary civil standard.

D. Attorney fees on appeal

Mortensen v. Stewart Title Guar. Co., 149 Idaho 437, 235 P.3d 387 (2010): Reiterates that a party seeking fees must cite statutory or contractual authority; used to deny the Coffeys’ fee request for failing to properly ground it in authority.

I.C. § 6-202(3)(c): The Byrds/Trust sought fees as “defendants” to the trespass claim, but the Court held no final merits determination existed due to remand.

I.C. § 12-121: Denied because the Coffeys were not the prevailing party and the appeal was not deemed frivolous in any event.

3.2 Legal Reasoning

A. Ambiguity: “shore” can reasonably mean different things in context

The Court first resolved an important threshold: whether the deed was ambiguous. The Byrds/Trust argued “shore” was a surveying term of art defined by the Manual of Instructions for the Survey of the Public Lands of the United States (1947) (“the Manual”) and that Idaho survey practice incorporates that framework. The Coffeys (through expert testimony) argued “shore” was used only to help locate or describe pins and direction, not to extend title to the OHWM.

Applying C & G, Inc. v. Rule and Camp Easton Forever, Inc. v. Inland Nw. Council Boy Scouts of Am., the Court held that because two competing interpretations were reasonable, the deed was ambiguous as a matter of law. The Court also rejected the attempt to make the deed unambiguous by invoking (i) the Manual’s definition and (ii) monument-priority rules—treating both as interpretive tools that come into play only after ambiguity is found, rather than as part of the deed’s “plain language” itself.

B. The key doctrinal correction: do not import quiet-title burdens into antecedent declaratory deed construction

The central reversal rests on how the district court framed the evidentiary task. The district court treated the Byrds/Trust as parties “claiming ownership of property of which the legal title stands” in another, and therefore required “clear and convincing evidence” (citing Luce v. Marble) to prevail on “Quiet Title and Declaratory Relief.”

The Supreme Court’s point is sequential and structural:

Step 1 (Declaratory judgment): determine what the ambiguous deed conveyed—i.e., whose chain of title includes the disputed lakeside strip. That interpretive determination is a factual inquiry into intent and is governed by the ordinary civil standard: preponderance of the evidence (supported by Watkins v. Fed. Life Ins. Co., the contract-analogy in Bear Crest Ltd. LLC v. State ex rel. Idaho Transp. Dep't, and the burden used for contract interpretation in A&B Irrigation Dist. v. Idaho Dep't of Water Res.).

Step 2 (Quiet title / other claims): only after ownership is declared does it make sense to ask whether a party is attempting to overcome record title in another (and thus whether a heightened clear-and-convincing burden applies to that quiet-title theory), or whether trespass follows from an established ownership determination.

In short, the trial court “conflated” the burdens: it used the quiet-title evidentiary rule to decide the predicate question of deed meaning and ownership allocation. The Supreme Court treated that as reversible error because the wrong burden can change outcomes, especially when extrinsic evidence is mixed.

C. Why “harmless error” did not save the judgment

The district court stated that it would reach the same result even under a preponderance standard. The Supreme Court refused to accept that assurance because:

The district court’s reasoning was expressly built around the clear and convincing standard.

Its analysis addressed only a limited portion of the trial record (e.g., pin location and the Taylor-to-Chappell deed’s “together with” language).

It did not explain why the broader set of evidence (including deed exceptions referencing “mean high water line,” assessor treatment, survey practice testimony, and related deeds) failed under a preponderance framework.

Because the boundary determination was foundational to trespass liability and fee shifting, the Court also reversed the trespass award and attorney fees as derivative rulings.

3.3 Impact

A. Procedural impact on property and water-adjacency disputes

The decision clarifies a practical sequencing rule for Idaho real-property litigation: when the case turns on an ambiguous instrument, courts must first resolve ownership through declaratory interpretation under a preponderance standard before invoking heightened quiet-title burdens. This matters because many shoreline disputes are litigated as hybrids—declaratory judgment (meaning of deed), quiet title (title confirmation), and tort claims (trespass).

B. Substantive impact on littoral-rights litigation strategy

The opinion does not decide whether “shore” means OHWM in this deed, but it reshapes the litigation terrain:

Parties asserting littoral rights are less likely to face an improper heightened burden merely because the relief sought includes quiet title language.

Parties opposing littoral adjacency can still prevail, but must do so within the ordinary civil evidentiary framework when the question is deed intent/meaning.

Downstream claims (trespass, damages, fee awards) must await a correctly determined ownership baseline, reducing the risk that tort liability is imposed on an erroneously elevated standard for the predicate deed question.

C. Institutional impact: boundaries between administrative permitting and judicial title adjudication

Read alongside Byrd v. Idaho State Bd. of Land Comm'rs, the case continues a line separating (i) agency permitting decisions under lake protection laws from (ii) judicial adjudication of ownership and littoral rights. The permitting process cannot be used as a substitute for title litigation, and title litigation must apply the correct civil burdens when construing ambiguous conveyances.

4. Complex Concepts Simplified

Littoral rights: Rights of a landowner whose land borders a lake (e.g., access to the water, ability to seek certain encroachment permits), generally dependent on adjacency.

OHWM (Ordinary High Water Mark): The boundary line impressed on the shore by ordinary high-water conditions; for navigable waters, it often functions as the dividing line between private uplands and state-owned lakebed.

Ambiguous deed: A deed is ambiguous when its language is reasonably subject to more than one interpretation. If ambiguous, courts may consider extrinsic evidence (surrounding circumstances, related deeds, survey testimony) to find intent.

Declaratory judgment vs quiet title: Declaratory judgment declares parties’ rights (e.g., what a deed conveyed). Quiet title is a judgment that settles and confirms title as against adverse claims. This case stresses that the court must usually declare ownership first (deed meaning) before applying certain quiet-title evidentiary rules.

Preponderance vs clear and convincing evidence: Preponderance means “more likely than not.” Clear and convincing is a higher level of certainty. Applying the higher standard when the law requires the lower one can improperly tilt the fact-finding outcome.

Metes and bounds / pins / monuments: A deed may describe boundaries by bearings and distances to physical markers (iron pins). Natural features (like a shore) may also be referenced. When terms conflict or are unclear, courts use interpretive rules—after finding ambiguity—to decide what controls.

5. Conclusion

Byrd v. Coffey establishes a consequential procedural clarification for Idaho property litigation: when a court is asked to resolve an ambiguous deed through declaratory judgment to determine ownership (and thus littoral adjacency), it must apply the ordinary civil burden—preponderance of the evidence—before turning to heightened quiet-title proof rules. The decision reinforces disciplined sequencing in mixed claims (declaration, quiet title, trespass), ensures burdens match the nature of the issue being tried, and underscores the centrality of correct deed-interpretation methodology in shoreline disputes where a narrow strip of land can determine substantial lake-use rights.

title: Faith leaders, activists rally around immigrants after Columbus ICE activity
description:

text:
Several local faith leaders and activists are strongly speaking out and expressing solidarity with the area’s immigrant communities on the heels of what appears to be a protracted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation that’s occurred throughout the Columbus area — and all over the state — in recent days.

The reported ICE activity marks the first time the Hoosier state has seen the type of widespread crackdowns promised during the second Trump administration and seen in other states like Minnesota and Illinois in recent months.

The efforts are drawing different reactions from Indiana lawmakers. U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, R-Indiana, told Indianapolis TV station WTHR that “ICE is doing its job. They’re cracking down on illegals that are here who have been reported and doing their job to deport them and its incumbent on all of us leaders to support the mission of ICE.”

Meanwhile, U.S. Rep. Andre Carson, D-Indiana, submitted an official Congressional inquiry to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and ICE asking for more information.

“My district should not be forced to rely on bystander videos and media reports to understand the actions of federal agents operating in their communities,” Carson wrote. “Immigration enforcement must comply with the Constitution and protect public safety.”

Locally, after a video circulated on social media Wednesday showing what appeared to be ICE agents making an arrest just outside Camila’s Mexican Restaurant on 25th Street, Camila’s and a few other area Mexican restaurants closed early, including TaColumbus, citing fear on behalf of both employees and customers. In other parts of the state, several businesses also closed early, most prominently in Indianapolis.

Some, like Camila’s, opened the next day. Others, like TaColumbus, remained closed on Thursday, but reopened on Friday.

Camila’s in particular posted on social media that staff members were “completely speechless” regarding the amount of support received when business opened back up on Thursday.

“Words cannot express how grateful we are for the incredible love and warmth we received today,” a post from late Thursday reads.

Comments on social media posts made by businesses that closed temporarily were mainly filled with well-wishers and supporters too.

Activity, arrests reported on social media

During the Wednesday incident outside Camila’s, a purported ICE agent can be seen on video wearing a tactical vest with ERO emblazoned on it, with ERO referring to ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations directorate. Another video showed the agency performing a traffic stop on a vehicle on what appeared to be State Road 46 near Interstate 65.

While The Republic could not independently verify the video, the tactical vest worn by an individual in the footage appeared consistent with vests marked “ERO,” an acronym used by ICE’s ERO directorate in publicly available photographs.

Hours after the incident, a white van believed to have been driven by the person detained remained in the parking lot. No information about the individual has been released.

Unconfirmed reports of ICE making arrests continued through Thursday, with sightings on Jonathan Moore Pike, North National Road and U.S. 31 near Taylorsville, according to People over Papers, a crowdsourced website where people submit potential sightings of immigration agents. But sightings appeared to be more sparse Friday.

When The Republic contacted ICE on Wednesday about the reports of activity, asking whether the agency was conducting operations in the Bartholomew and Jackson County areas, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson did not answer the question. The spokesperson said that “ICE agents uphold our nation’s immigration laws in all 50 states, seven days a week, 24 hours a day,” before sending photos and names of a select group of people who the spokesperson said were “some of the worst of the worst arrested by ICE in Indiana.” The five people, who are from Mexico, Niger, Haiti and Honduras, were reportedly convicted of charges like kidnapping, identity theft, rape, child neglect and aggravated assault.

The response did not provide any information about where the five people were living in Indiana. It appears other Indiana media outlets were sent the same response after making inquiries.

It is unclear how many arrests have been made locally. The Republic reached out to ICE again on Friday, noting outlets received the same response and asking for information about the number of arrests locally or how long the operation would last, but did not hear back by press time.

The city of Columbus, for its part, issued a statement Wednesday evening stating neither Mayor Mary Ferdon’s administration nor the Columbus Police Department received any prior notice about the operation and were unaware it was taking place. The statement went on to note that, in accordance with local policies, CPD is not involved in any federal immigration control operations and has not signed any agreements with federal law enforcement to participate in such actions.

“We remain committed to keeping everyone informed and safe, and we will share verified updates as soon as we have more information,” the statement concludes.

The Bartholomew County Sheriff’s Office was not officially made aware of any ICE activity in the county, and they did not request its assistance, per Lt. Dane Duke, a sheriff’s office spokesperson.

‘People are frightened’

Rev. Felipe Martinez, pastor of First Presbyterian Church and an advocate for immigrant communities, said when he first heard that ICE was in the community that he was filled with concern.

“ICE has a documented pattern of making arrests in a brutal fashion, and I didn’t want that for my neighbors,” Martinez told The Republic. “It is also documented that over 70% of the people who are being detained do not have a criminal record at all. And I was afraid of people getting swept up without reason. I was deeply troubled and concerned for the families that will lose a wage earner, caregivier, supporter, relative because of these detentions.”

“People are frightened because ICE is an unaccountable agency,” the pastor went on. “I hear people say on social media, ‘If you haven’t done anything wrong, you have nothing to be fearful about.’ Well, tell that to the family of U.S. citizens who’ve been killed by ICE.”

Martinez noted the “We Stand With Our Immigrant Neighbors” signs that First Presbyterian Church and Columbus Area Arts Council began producing last year.

“I’m looking for our community to express not sadness, but indignation,” Martinez said. “I want us to be thinking: ‘Is this the country we want?’”

Just last weekend, Martinez spoke at an interfaith prayer vigil on the steps of Columbus City Hall speaking out against what they described as “brutal conditions” that ICE detainees suffer through in Indiana, particularly at the Miami Correction Facility just north of Kokomo where two ICE detainees have died since the beginning of this year.

Martinez called the events of the past week “a staggering situation to be living under” but said he was proud of how people have stepped up to support immigrant-owned businesses.

“We cannot stand idly by and pretend this doesn’t impact all of us. I believe that the community can express support in a healthy way, in a courageous way, in a peaceful way — with a message not for ICE, but a message for our neighbors,” Martinez said. “I want our neighbors to know that we stand by them and with them. Immigrants are our neighbors. They’re not the enemy. Put political rhetoric aside and immigration debate aside; this is about instilling fear in a community, and I will not have it.”

ICE presence ‘very unexpected’

Su Casa, a Latino-focused nonprofit social-service organization, has been putting out information reminding people of their constitutionally enshrined rights if they were to be stopped by ICE, as well as important documents for them to have on hand during this time.

Su Casa is trying to raise $30,000 that will go towards a client emergency support fund to help immigrant families in Bartholomew, Jackson and Shelby counties with urgent needs that pays for things like Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) renewal fees, rent, utilities, medical bills, legal fees and more. That $30,000 goal would match a $30,000 grant Su Casa received through the UnidosUS Affiliate Emergency Relief Fund.

Brandon Santillan-Fuentes, a family support specialist at Su Casa, said the organization has been receiving an influx of calls from scared people, and that they have been urging families to stay inside if they are fearful.

“It’s an unfortunate event, but people should stay calm and be ready,” Santillan-Fuentes said. “We’re getting a lot of fear.”

The presence of ICE in Columbus was “very unexpected” and happened “very fast,” he said, adding that the community “was not expecting them (ICE) to come to Columbus this hard.”

Johnnie Edwards, president of local NAACP Branch 3071 and a pastor at Abundant Harvest Ministries International in Columbus, said that as an area that likes to think of itself as a place of community, now is the time to follow through on that.

“I’m a firm believer that we can’t build a safe community by terrorizing people who live in this community. They shouldn’t be afraid to go to work or school, because at that point, when one suffers, we all suffer,” Edwards said. “… A lot of people in this community say they’re believers of Christ, but are we Christ-like? Are we doing things that represent what we truly believe in? I’m hoping that we as a community, come together and do the very things that we say we believe in.”

Mary Cartwright, a local organizer and retired Methodist pastor, speaking on behalf of Bartholomew County Indivisible and Columbus Community United, two local grassroots activist groups, said she was “appalled that ICE is here in the county.”

“Nobody’s arguing that there shouldn’t be any ICE enforcement,” she said. “It just shouldn’t be this way.”

text:
A federal appeals court has ruled to keep in place a lower court blockade on the Department of Homeland Security using its SAVE database to check voter rolls, undercutting the Trump administration’s efforts to help states boot noncitizens from their registration lists.

The U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia, in a 2-1 decision, said the database — officially known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements — can spit back false negatives, or cases where it wrongly identifies a citizen as a noncitizen.

And expanding use of the database, which was created to figure out if an immigrant was eligible for welfare, to mass-checks of voter rolls violates the Privacy Act, the court said. The judges said it would mean sharing Social Security numbers outside of the contours of the law.

In an unsigned opinion, the two-judge majority — both of them Obama appointees — said the lower court blockade will remain in place while the case develops.

“The public interest does not favor interim restoration of a system the government has not made a strong showing it may lawfully operate,” the judges said.

Dissenting was Judge Gregory Katsas, a Trump appointee, who said he would have allowed states to continue using the SAVE database for voter roll checks.

Judge Katsas said the false negatives — citizens who are flagged as noncitizens because they never updated their records after naturalization — have an easy solution. They just have to provide proof of citizenship to remain on the rolls.

He also dismissed the idea that the expanded SAVE system tramples on privacy, saying the Social Security numbers would be shared with DHS but wouldn’t be made public.

Judge Katsas also said the federal government has a significant interest in using SAVE to help cleanse voter rolls.

“The government will suffer irreparable harm absent a stay,” Judge Katsas ruled.

DHS expanded use of the SAVE system last year, linking new databases and allowing states to run large batches of names, at no cost. The Biden administration had resisted those changes.

The system is part of a broader push by the Trump administration on voting. The administration argues that noncitizens and other ineligible voters are casting ballots and skewing elections.

Indeed, the Justice Department on Friday announced it had charged four immigrants — two of them here illegally and the others with some legal status — with casting illegal votes in the 2022 and 2024 elections.

The president’s opponents say the focus on cleansing voter rolls risks booting valid voters, hindering their own right to vote.

The Washington case isn’t the only one involving the SAVE system.

Judge Katsas pointed out that another federal district court in Florida has ruled that a previous settlement between some GOP-led states and the federal government requires DHS to make SAVE available for voter checks.

Judge Katsas said it’s impossible to square that with the ruling by the district court in Washington that imposed the blockade.

The two other judges, though, said the matter wasn’t that clear.

They said the Florida ruling has been appealed to another circuit court, which is deciding how to square the two cases.

text:
At a mandatory training, US judges were told to reduce time given to people awaiting visas or green cards before being deported.

A Guardian report claimed that immigration judges across the US have been asked to be strict and deny people time as they wait for their Green Cards so that they can be deported. A mandatory training for judges also urged them to threaten attorneys who accept too many immigration cases. “There is no room to be kind; there is only urgency to make them leave [the US], one way or the other," the judges were told. Citing sources, the Guardian report claimed that hundreds of immigration judges attended a mandatory presentation in recent days about “continuances” – a legal tool which has historically been used to give immigrants more time to find lawyers, build their cases or wait for approval of their applications for documents at another federal immigration agency. The virtual training session was led by a veteran immigration judge, Keith Hunsucker, of the Board of immigration appeals, the immigration courts’ appellate branch. He denied over 80% of asylum cases for much of the time that he was on the bench in immigration court before moving on to other roles, the report said. The training was apparently meant to reduce the immigration court backlog and they were taught that some continuances are sought solely for the purpose of delay and persons illegally present in the United States who wish to remain have a substantial incentive to prolong litigation so they may avoid deportation as long as possible. Continuance requests solely for dilatory purposes should not be countenanced by Immigration Judges,” one slide read An approved visa petition should not delay deportation proceedings if the visa itself is not yet available because of annual quotas but would be issued to the qualified recipient at a later, albeit unspecified, date, the training suggested. Though there is a huge backlog, the judges were told during the training that immigration attorneys risk punitive measures for accepting what are deemed too many cases. “Where a practitioner takes on more cases than he or she can responsibly and professionally handle,” one of the slides read, “it may be appropriate for an Immigration Judge to consider referral to EOIR disciplinary counsel for further action and possible sanction for a violation. ”

End of Article

description:
