Quantifying the Economic Impact of 2025 ICE Raids on California’s Agricultural Industry: A Case Study of Oxnard.
text:
By Jessie Chen and Caleb Bergeron | Spring 2026 – Volume 16

Introduction

Since the return of the Trump administration, the

United States has seen a sharp escalation in

immigration enforcement. In May 2025, Trump’s

adviser Stephen Miller publicly stated that DHS has a

target of 3,000 daily arrests (Olivares, 2025), and by

November 2025, the number has increased by over

75% in a year (Melnick, 2026). These intensified

crackdowns have reached deep into factories, farms,

construction sites, and service-sector workplaces.

Beyond removing migrants from employment, they

have also created fear among workers, leading many to

avoid workdays (Ma, 2025). This paper focuses on the

economic consequences of this enforcement, a topic

that demands more rigorous attention than it has

received. First, it examines the impact of ICE

enforcement on the agricultural and construction labor

markets. Second, it analyzes the fiscal costs of ICE

enforcement and the reduction in the labor supply.

Finally, it assesses the impact of the disruptions in

labor growth and participation from ICE enforcement.

Background

Economists have long debated how immigration

affects wages. Economist George Borjas (2013)

observed that an influx of low-skilled immigrant labor

places downward pressure on wages for low-skilled

native workers, acting as a short-term supply shock

that increases labor supply faster than capital

adjustment. By contrast, David Card (1990, 2016)

suggests a statistically insignificant average wage effect,

or even a slightly positive one, because immigrant

labor is often an imperfect substitute for native labor

and can increase efficiency through specialization and

complementarities in production. The debate between

these two positions has never been fully resolved.

In this context, however, we wonder the reverse question:

what happens to labor markets when that immigrant

workforce is suddenly removed? To discuss this outcome,

we observe two specific industries. Let’s start with

agriculture.

Agricultural Impact

Farmers are disproportionately affected by Migration

enforcement. Over the past decade, some 40% of the crop

labor force has been undocumented (Gutiérrez, 2025).

Compare that to the 19.2% of foreign born that account

for the civilian labor force (U.S. Bureau of Labor

Statistics, 2024). The roots of migrant dependence trace

back several decades. After the United States eliminated

lawful pathways for seasonal agricultural labor in the

1960s, undocumented migration surged in the 1970s. Over

time, employers continued to require large numbers of

workers, and migrants increasingly settled permanently in

local communities to fill low-wage jobs (Shashkevich,

2018). With few legal pathways for entry, a sudden surge in

ICE arrests, and widespread fear of showing up to work,

migrant labor is not as reliable as it used to be.

We see that through added labor costs and reduced output

for farmers in the short run (Charlton, 2025). According

to the 2022 USDA Census, wages and salaries represented

42% of production expenses for greenhouse and nursery

operations, and 40% for fruit and tree nut operations

(USDA, 2025).

Without a new stream of migrant workers, and with many

well established communities being targeted, agricultural

systems must rapidly change. In the short run, where

harvest seasons are time sensitive, firms that depend on

this labor will have to face reduced productivity and/or

higher production costs (Charlton, 2025).

In the long run, the effect is expected to be less drastic. If

these ICE enforcements were to continue, the laborintensive

farmers eventually must turn towards

technological innovations and large-scale capital-intensive

farming techniques (Charlton, 2025). The US has already

gravitated towards technological innovation in agriculture

since the 1950s, which has reduced the need for

farmworkers significantly (USDA, 2025). Increased farm

yields and mechanization over the past few decades have

substituted the need for human labor. Historically, any

long run effect of a migrant labor shock is quite small

compared to any short run effect, as farmers respond by

investing in capital improvements to ensure productivity

gains.

For the average American grocery shopper, the most

tangible question is whether the agricultural labor

disruption translates into a rise in food prices. In the short

run, farmers, not consumers, will absorb most of the

shock. Farmers typically bear the cost of price variability

because consumer demand for agricultural goods is more

elastic than producer supply (Mitchell, 2022). Not only do

domestic producers face foreign competition for a virtually

identical product, but consumers can substitute for

alternative agricultural goods much easier than farmers

can. Consider almonds, one of California’s most laborintensive

crops: a 1% increase in price leads to a 1.0464%

decrease in quantity demanded, while the same price

increase yields only a 0.64% increase in quantity supplied

(Bakhtavoryan, 2022). But the risk of food supply

disruption still exists. In Oxnard, California, analysis by

Xinyu Li estimates a 20–40% reduction in the agricultural

workforce, leading to $3–7 billion in crop losses and a 5–

12% increase in produce prices (Li, 2025). This implies that

while farmers may absorb much of the immediate shock,

sustained labor shortages can disproportionately impact

the price of labor-intensive crops in the short run. The

same labor supply shocks are also present in the

construction industry.

Impact on Construction

While agriculture only comprises about 1.9% of foreignborn

jobs, construction compromises 9.9% of foreignborn

jobs (U.S. Census, n.d.). The proportion of

undocumented workers in the construction industry is

likely larger; some predictions say 20% of the

construction workforce is undocumented (University of

Michigan, 2024). At the same time, it’s worth noting that

the Census reports that 8.1% of the foreign-born

population is self-employed in a non-incorporated

business (U.S. Census, n.d.). The nature of

subcontracting in construction implies that many of

those classified as self-employed on the census and

acting as “independent contractors” are still working in

construction (University of Michigan, 2024). Moreover,

US Immigration law encourages such subcontracting,

penalizing firms that knowingly hire migrant labor

(S.1200, 1986).

Neither of these industries comprises a very large part

of the total foreign-born population workforce (Service,

Management, and Education are the top three) (U.S.

Census, n.d.). However, much like agriculture, this

is an industry that reports disproportionate targeting

from ICE.

In 2024, foreign born workers were more likely to be

employed in construction occupations than native

workers (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024). At the

same time, although without correlation, a survey by the

Associated General Contractors of America says that

“Over 92% of construction firms report having a hard

time finding workers to hire”. Around 5% of

respondents to that survey reported direct visits from

immigration agents, leading to project delays

(Construction Workforce Shortages, 2025). This makes

issues of affordability worse, as the construction

industry is already suffering from systemic project delays

(Construction Workforce Shortages, 2025).

The problem of the construction worker

shortage, much like that of the

agricultural worker shortage, is

multifaceted. Immigration

enforcement is only one small

part of construction worker

shortage.

Projects are being delayed in the short term because of

ICE enforcement. This is in part because many migrant

workers now face heightened risks in simply showing up

to work. Even if a small proportion of the total migrant

population gets arrested, the cost of getting arrested is

severe. For many workers, the lost wage is far less costly

than being placed in an ICE detention facility. For firms

that depend on these workers for construction projects,

that translates into a loss of productivity. This goes to

show that the cost of ICE isn’t just limited to migrant

workers, but its economic impact is borne by firms as

well.

Impact on Government Revenues

Beyond the labor market, ICE enforcement carries a

direct fiscal cost to American taxpayers. Americans pay

for ICE directly through increased spending and

decreased revenue. A 4-year policy would increase

primary deficits by about $270 billion while a 10-year

policy would cost about $862 billion (Davis et al., 2024).

At the same time, there is a loss in government tax

revenue from deported migrants. As taxpayers,

undocumented immigrants make great contributions to

public finances. In 2022, they paid 26.1% of their

income in taxes, a rate nearly identical to the amount

paid by the median U.S. household (26.4%) (Davis et al.,

2024). This contribution is especially significant because

undocumented immigrants generally have limited access

to public benefits despite paying into the system. For

instance, spending on emergency Medicaid for

undocumented immigrants accounted for less than 1%

of overall Medicaid spending between fiscal years 2017

and 2023 (JAMA Research Letter, 2025). In other words,

mass deportation is a costly fiscal choice that asks

taxpayers to fund expanded enforcement while forfeiting

billions in existing tax contributions.

Further Discussion

Throughout this discussion of labor force participation,

fear is a driving factor. This fear does not discriminate

cleanly between the documented and undocumented. As

ICE operations have expanded, reports of people being

stopped or detained based on appearance rather than

verified status has caused even documented immigrants

and legal residents in immigrant communities to reduce

their public activity.

According to a KFF report published in November

2025, about three in ten immigrants report avoiding

traveling, seeking medical care, or going to work or other

public spaces (Valdes et al., 2025). Workers are

withdrawing from the labor market, and we observe

decreased labor-force participation in the short run.

During the week of June 8th–14th, California’s labor

force participation rate fell by 3.1% as ICE carried out

large-scale raids in Los Angeles and elsewhere in the

state, even as participation in the rest of the country rose

by 0.5% (Flores et al., 2025). At a national level, the U.S.

foreign-born labor force declined by 1.2 million from

January to July 2025 (Anderson, 2025). Although the

evidence is indirect, it suggests potential disruptions in

the labor market, since immigrants have contributed

more than half of U.S. labor force growth in each of the

last three decades.

Summary

In summary, undocumented immigrants strengthen the

U.S. economy as consumers, taxpayers, and workers.

Their spending supports local businesses. Their tax

contributions benefit public budgets. Their labor

increases productivity and reduces prices for producers.

This in effect points to one reality: the cost of ICE is far

more than just its budget. Large-scale deportations have

rapidly restructured major US industries, state and local

revenue, and consumer spending. For both domestic

firms and migrant communities, migratory labor is

rapidly changing in response to ICE. Thus any policy

that overlooks these economic interdependencies risks

undermining the very stability it attempts to protect.

text:
Denmark and four other European Union countries agreed Friday on a model for "return hubs" in non-EU nations and hope to begin sending migrants to the facilities as early as 2027, an official said Friday.

The announcement, made after a one-day meeting in Copenhagen, is the latest development in an effort by EU states to send people whose asylum requests have been rejected to third countries outside the bloc.

"We are moving forward toward what is actually a fundamental transformation of the common European migration and asylum system," said Morten Bødskov, Denmark's minister of immigration and integration.

He briefed reporters alongside counterparts from Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece. The five countries have been negotiating with governments mainly in Africa over potential sites, pioneering the initiative for the whole of the EU.

Human rights groups have criticized plans to deport migrants to centers or prisons in third countries, arguing European nations cannot guarantee their rights will be respected there.

Bødskov rejected the idea that "return hubs" were a euphemism for detention and deportation centers and said the International Organization for Migration and the U.N. Refugee Agency would monitor the centers.

"We are not talking about camps, we are talking about opportunities, for a new chance for irregular migrants who cannot return to their own country today and who have no legal grounds to be in our countries," Bødskov said.

The UNHCR told The Associated Press it "has not been approached with details of such a proposal," and therefore "cannot comment on the specific arrangements being discussed or on what any potential role for UNHCR might entail."

IOM told the AP no decision had been made on IOM's potential role in "return hubs." "Discussions remain exploratory," and IOM had provided only "technical advice to some EU Member States on safeguards and operational considerations."

"We have consistently underscored that any such initiative must comply with EU regulatory and legal frameworks, protect migrants' rights, respect partner countries' interests, and ensure individuals' access to meaningful, sustainable solutions," an IOM spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

Although the ministers did not specify which third countries were being considered, Bødskov said they expect to reach their first deal by early 2027.

He acknowledged the concept of "return hubs" was mocked only a few years ago and deemed incompatible with EU and international law.

EU laws, however, have changed due to public and political pressure for tougher measures against irregular migration.

European lawmakers voted in June to allow member states to set up centers outside the EU on their own or in small coalitions, and send rejected asylum seekers there instead of to their home countries.

"This is something new and it's groundbreaking," said Bart van den Brink, the Netherlands' minister of asylum and migration.

In early August, a spokesperson for the Rwandan government said it "was natural" for her government to negotiate with European countries and others to potentially host asylum seekers who are not allowed to live elsewhere.

Speaking to Royal FM Kigali, Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo cited an emergency transit mechanism established in Gashora in 2018 for people evacuated from Libya, who could stay there until they were resettled in third countries.

Makolo said one of the ideas discussed was to offer a "safe place" where people who have nowhere else to go could get medical care, training and rest while their asylum applications were processed.

It remained unclear what countries in negotiations with EU nations would gain in return for taking Europe's rejected migrants.

Migrant rights groups have criticized European efforts to set up migrant centers abroad where it may be difficult to monitor and enforce human rights.

In an emailed statement, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, said "vague assurances of compliance with human rights law are not enough."

The European ministers in Copenhagen emphasized the new hubs would abide by European and international law.

Van den Brink, the Dutch immigration minister, said technical talks and missions to potential partner countries would be used "to gain more insight into the human rights situation and the living conditions of the refugees."

Information for this article was contributed by Philipp Jenne and Sam McNeil of The Associated Press.

title: Five EU countries plan return hubs for rejected migrants, facing criticism from rights groups
description:
Denmark and four other EU countries announced on Friday that they are establishing “return hubs” in non-EU nations, with plans to start sending migrants to these facilities as early as 2027.
Human rights groups have criticised the plans, fearing that deporting migrants to third-country centres could compromise their rights.
The IOM confirmed that no decision has been made regarding its role in “return hubs,” noting that discussions are still exploratory.
Rights groups concerned about “return hubs” Migrant rights groups have criticised EU plans to set up migrant centres abroad.
In an emailed statement, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O’Flaherty said, “vague assurances of compliance with human rights law are not enough.” “States need to commit to the guardrails necessary to prevent setting up human rights black holes,“ he said.
text:
Denmark and four other EU countries announced on Friday that they are establishing “return hubs” in non-EU nations, with plans to start sending migrants to these facilities as early as 2027. Morten Bødskov, Denmark’s Minister of Immigration and Integration, described this initiative as a fundamental transformation of the European migration and asylum system.

Denmark, alongside Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece, is in negotiations with primarily African governments about potential locations for these hubs. Human rights groups have criticised the plans, fearing that deporting migrants to third-country centres could compromise their rights.

Bødskov countered claims that “return hubs” are simply detention centres, stating that the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) and the UN Refugee Agency will oversee the facilities. He emphasised that these hubs offer new opportunities for irregular migrants unable to return to their home countries.

The UNHCR told The Associated Press it has not received details about the proposal and cannot comment on potential arrangements. The IOM confirmed that no decision has been made regarding its role in “return hubs,” noting that discussions are still exploratory. An IOM spokesperson stated that any initiative must comply with EU regulations, protect migrants’ rights, respect partner countries’ interests, and ensure access to sustainable solutions.

Although ministers did not specify which third countries were under consideration, Bødskov stated they expect to finalise their first agreement by early 2027. The concept of “return hubs,” previously mocked as incompatible with EU and international law, is now gaining traction due to public and political pressure for stricter measures against irregular migration.

In June, European lawmakers voted to allow member states to create centres outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers rather than sending them back to their home countries. Bart van den Brink, the Netherlands’ minister of asylum and migration, called this approach groundbreaking.

Negotiations with Rwanda to host asylum seekers

In early August, a Rwandan government spokesperson stated that it was “natural” to negotiate with European countries to host asylum seekers who cannot live elsewhere. Yolande Makolo mentioned an emergency transit mechanism established in Gashora in 2018 for individuals evacuated from Libya, allowing them to remain until they are resettled in another country.

She explained that discussions included providing a “safe place” for those in need, as well as offering medical care and training while their asylum applications were processed. “We want to be part of a solution to a significant global problem,” Makolo said. However, it remains unclear what benefits countries negotiating with the EU would receive for accepting rejected migrants from Europe.

Rights groups concerned about “return hubs”

Migrant rights groups have criticised EU plans to set up migrant centres abroad. They suggest it may be difficult to monitor and enforce human rights.

In an emailed statement, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O’Flaherty said, “vague assurances of compliance with human rights law are not enough.”

“States need to commit to the guardrails necessary to prevent setting up human rights black holes,“ he said.

At the meeting in Copenhagen, European ministers confirmed that the new hubs would comply with European and international law. Dutch immigration minister Van den Brink noted that discussions and missions to potential partner countries would help assess the human rights situation and living conditions of refugees. He emphasised the importance of aligning their approach with European values and human rights.

“EU leaders may call these centres an ‘innovative solution,‘ but outsourcing migration control is an old tactic to simply move people out of sight and evade human rights obligations,“ director of Brussels-based rights group PICUM Michele LeVoy said.

This article used information from The Associated Press.

Guyana says that it has received six people deported from the United States, as the administration of President Donald Trump steps up so-called third-country deportations.

Guyana’s Foreign Secretary Robert Persaud announced that a group of Cuban and Afghan nationals had arrived in the South American nation on Saturday, after being deported due to immigration issues.

“The US has not made any further requests” for non-citizen deportations to be sent to Guyana at this time, Persaud told The Associated Press news agency.

None had criminal backgrounds, according to Persaud. The removals are part of an ongoing campaign under Trump, who promised during his 2024 re-election bid to engineer the “largest deportation programme of criminals in the history of America”.

Persaud said that Guyana reached an agreement with the US to receive deportees after months of negotiations.

The human rights nonprofit Amnesty International estimates that more than 30 countries have entered into such agreements since Trump returned to office, including 15 in the Americas region.

The deal with Guyana will last for one year and does not constitute permanent resettlement, Persaud said.

Third-country deportations involve sending foreign nationals to places outside of their country of origin. Deportees often have no familiarity with the country they are sent to and sometimes do not even speak the language.

The Trump administration has sought to expand the use of third-country deportations.

It has struck agreements with a range of countries around the world, including several as far afield as Africa. Some of the deals have involved multimillion-dollar payments.

Trump officials have justified the effort by arguing that some countries, such as Cuba, refuse to accept deportees from the US.

Rights groups, however, have denounced the practice as an effort to punish migrants and pressure them into giving up their immigration claims in the US.

Many of the deportees have no criminal background, reflecting the expanding scope of Trump’s deportation efforts during his second term.

The Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), a research organisation at Syracuse University, estimates that 70.6 percent of foreign nationals currently in US immigration detention have no criminal conviction.

Third-country deportations have also raised concerns about conditions in the countries non-citizens are sent to. Some countries struggle with poverty, instability and conflict, as well as human rights abuses.

The deportees sent to Guyana on Saturday will receive resources through the Assisted Voluntary Return Programme, run by the United Nations International Organisation for Migration (IOM).

Under the arrangement, those deported will await the outcome of their immigration process in Guyana.

They could return to their countries of origin or seek relocation elsewhere.

Efforts to restrict immigration, deport foreign nationals and crack down on civil immigration infractions have become a hallmark of Trump’s second term.

As part of that campaign, the Trump administration has stripped tens of thousands of migrants in the country of their legal status, through the cancellation of programmes like Temporary Protected Status or humanitarian parole.

Reports have also emerged that the administration plans to strip visas from roughly 200,000 people seeking asylum.

The removal of their legal immigration status exposes foreign nationals to the risk of deportation, in some cases despite ongoing conflicts or unstable conditions in their destination countries.

text:
Guyana on Friday became the latest "third country" to accept migrants deported from the United States, a U.S. official told CBS News.

The South American country received a handful of Afghan and Cuban deportees expelled by the Trump administration, the official said.

Guyana is one of more than 30 nations that have now signed deals with the Trump administration to accept deportees from the U.S. who are not their own citizens.

The Guyanese government said in a statement that those relocated to the country under what it called the "Assisted Voluntary Return Program" will await the outcome of their immigration cases in Guyana. They could ultimately return to their country of origin or be relocated somewhere else.

The U.N. International Organization for Migration is responsible for implementing the program, authorities in Guyana said, adding that the government will not bear any housing or support costs.

Guyana's Foreign Secretary Robert Persaud told the Associated Press on Saturday that six nationals from Cuba and Afghanistan arrived on Friday after being vetted by his administration and found to have no criminal backgrounds.

Persaud said his administration reached an agreement to host the deportees after months of negotiations. He also told the AP that "the U.S. has not made any further requests." The arrangement will run for a year and does not constitute permanent resettlement, he said.

Guyana, a founding member of the 15-nation Caribbean Community, is the latest of several member states to have received small groups of U.S. deportees. Others include St. Kitts and Nevis, Belize and St. Lucia, which was due to accept its first group this week, officials said.

Human rights activists have denounced the third-country deportations as inhumane and illegal under international law, saying some countries are returning deportees to places they fled because of persecution.

But the Trump administration has defended the legality and merits of the deportations, portraying them as an effective way to deter illegal immigration.

authors: Zack Kligler, Megan Rose, Andy Mannix, Mike Ludwig, Ibrahim Hirsi, Sharon Zhang, Ariana Figueroa, Amy Goodman, Juan González, Shireen Akram-Boshar

text:
Over the “strongest possible” objections from the federal prosecutor handling the case, leaders at the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., quashed plans to bring civil rights charges against an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent accused of shooting a Venezuelan immigrant and then lying about it.

The agent, 52-year-old Christian Castro, allegedly shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg in Minneapolis this January during Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration’s immigration blitz that sent thousands of federal agents into the state. The incident was one of three shootings by immigration agents in the city, the other two of which were fatal.

Federal prosecutors in Minnesota had been preparing to charge Castro with deprivation of rights under color of law for the shooting of Sosa-Celis, according to several people familiar with the case. Those charges are similar to the ones leveled against Minneapolis police officers accused in George Floyd’s killing and can carry hefty prison sentences.

Late on Tuesday, Matthew Evans, the assistant U.S. attorney in Minnesota in charge of the case, told lawyers for Sosa-Celis and other victims to prepare for Castro to be charged “only with False Statements,” according to an email that was reviewed by ProPublica.

That charge would likely carry a far less severe punishment if he were convicted.

“This is being directed by the Main Justice and the US Attorney,” Evans wrote in a remarkably candid account of internal deliberations. “I objected in the strongest possible terms and fought it as hard as I could. It wasn’t enough.”

He wrote that the false statement charges could come soon and would likely be filed under seal.

“It has been an honor and a privilege to try to get justice for your clients,” Evans concluded the email.

A DOJ official said civil rights charges require consultation with the civil rights division in Washington, and “any charging decisions that come out of such investigations are collaborative and deliberative and adhere to the facts and law of that specific case and controversy.”

The agency “has not yet reached a conclusion on this matter and will never rush an investigative process and the thorough review of all evidence,” the official said.

Evans and a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Minnesota declined to comment. An attorney for Sosa-Celis did not return phone calls from a reporter. Castro, who has an outstanding warrant in Minnesota for this case, could not be reached for comment.

Under the Trump administration, the Justice Department’s civil rights division has been thinned and has dropped some Biden-era oversight of law enforcement agencies. This move by the DOJ is likely to fuel further concerns that the department is operating more in support of President Donald Trump’s political agenda than to preserve the rule of law. Earlier this year, a ProPublica analysis found that in almost every instance of immigration agents shooting people, Trump’s administration blamed the injured and dead within hours of the incident. In many of those cases, federal or local police declined to investigate the agents.

Castro, who was put on leave by the Department of Homeland Security, is also facing multiple state felony charges in Minnesota, including assault with a dangerous weapon. After he left Minneapolis and returned to Texas, Minnesota officials had requested state officials there extradite Castro to face the charges, but Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to cooperate. Castro had been held for 90 days in jail while the two states fought over the extradition. He was released last week.

Sosa-Celis was shot on Jan. 14, as Castro and another ICE agent chased Alfredo Aljorna, an immigrant from Venezuela, after a traffic stop. Aljorna ran to his home, which he shared with Sosa-Celis. The two men made it inside after a brief scramble, and Castro fired through the closed door, “knowing [the home] was occupied by several people,” according to state charging documents. One witness said there were two children in the house when Castro shot into it. Sosa-Celis was hit in the leg.

ICE agents then deployed tear gas into the home and took the men and their partners into custody, according to the documents and other court records.

DHS originally said Castro and the other agent were ambushed by the men and beaten with a shovel or broomstick, making Castro fear for his life and fire in self-defense. DHS called Sosa-Celis and Aljorna “violent criminal illegal aliens,” and federal prosecutors charged them with assault.

The next month, however, they dropped the charges against both men, and the DHS backed off its narrative in a rare admission of possible wrongdoing of its officers. “Video evidence has revealed the sworn testimony of the two agents appeared to be false,” then-acting ICE director Todd Lyons said in a statement.

After Castro’s release from jail, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who is leading the state’s prosecution against him, said she worried that Castro will flee to Mexico.

Reached for comment Wednesday, Moriarty compared the Justice Department’s decision to overrule Evans to its actions after ICE agents killed Renee Good. A week before shooting Sosa-Celis, ICE agent Jonathan Ross shot Good in her car. Agents alleged she drove toward them, but video of the incident showed Good’s wheels turned away from them when they shot her. Federal authorities first agreed to a joint investigation, but Justice Department officials later refused to cooperate with state police, deeming any review of the fatal shooting unnecessary.

text:
The Vietnam War veterans suing over President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch are seeking an emergency court order to block the administration from pursuing its imminent plans to break ground in the Washington D.C. area.

Veterans Michael Lemmon, Shaun Byrnes, Jon Gundersen — along with architectural historian Calder Loth — filed their temporary restraining order request shortly after Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced that project excavation would begin within the next two weeks.

Continuing their months-long legal battle with the president, the group is now claiming the Trump administration is unlawfully moving ahead with the arch without receiving necessary approval, namely that of Congress.

“Preserving Congress’s role in authorizing the design and siting of commemorative works and other structures on federal land in our national capital will ensure democratic accountability,” their lawyers wrote Friday.

The four first challenged the project in a February lawsuit attempting to halt efforts to construct the 250-foot arch, which Trump said would be the largest in the world. The National Park Service recently backed its proposed Memorial Circle location — across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial.

Lemmon, Byrnes, Gundersen and Loth also arguing the large arch would obscure historical sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House. In early August, the National Park Service (NPS) found the monument would have “adverse effects” on several historic sites as well as the skyline of the nation’s capital.

Their lawyers on Friday accused the administration of trying to move quickly enough to make the arch a “fait accompli” before U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan can determine whether the project is lawful.

The administration clarified the work planned for the next two weeks will consist of an archaeological survey involving four test pits to help the NPS comply with preservation requirements, rather than actual construction activity.

“This activity is not construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, of an arch,” the administration said in a legal filing submitted Friday.

Chutkan previously ordered the administration to provide 14 days’ notice before beginning construction.

The arch has received preliminary approval, but not final approval, from the National Capital Planning Commission. A historic preservation review is also underway.

title: Migration as Hybrid Coercion - Hungarian Conservative
description:
A Tactic with a History The term ‘weaponized migration’ is used most often in policy conversations, but laypeople often confuse it with irregular migration in general.
Treating weaponized migration as merely a more organized version of ‘regular’ irregular migration leads to the wrong policies.
As a result, fluctuations in arrivals at Ceuta and Melilla are probably the clearest available indicator of Morocco’s willingness to manage migration pressure.
During the 2015 migration crisis, Budapest was among the first to say that large-scale irregular migration was not merely a humanitarian issue but also about sovereignty, border security, and state capacity.
EU migration laws should recognize coerced migration as a separate category.
text:
This article was originally published in Vol. 6 No. 2 of our print edition.

In February 2020, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan stood before the cameras and announced that Türkiye would no longer stop migrants from crossing into Europe. ‘The gates are now open’, he declared.1 Within hours, Turkish authorities were transporting people by the thousands toward the Greek border at Evros. Clashes and injuries were reported, and Greek border forces, backed by Frontex, responded with force. Across the chancelleries of Europe, officials worked quickly to respond to something their legal provisions had not been designed to address: a neighbouring government deliberately routing human beings toward their borders as an act of foreign policy.

This was not a typical humanitarian crisis. It was more like a demonstration: a message sent through people and borders. The Turkish president was not surprised by what happened. He wanted to show that Europe’s external border could serve as a pressure valve and that Ankara controlled it. Most European leaders avoided saying this directly. Their reluctance makes sense, even if it is difficult to justify. Admitting that desperate people were being used as a tool to apply pressure would mean facing a hard truth: the same principles that shape Europe’s moral identity—including the right to asylum, protection of refugees, and open borders—were being used against them by those who do not share these values. That uncomfortable reality is the focus of this essay.

A Tactic with a History

The term ‘weaponized migration’ is used most often in policy conversations, but laypeople often confuse it with irregular migration in general. The difference between these terms, however, is important. Most people who cross European borders without permission do so because of poverty, conflict, or persecution—not because a government has planned their journey for political reasons. Weaponized migration means a state deliberately moves people to put pressure on another government or to gain a political advantage.2 In these cases, the migrants are not acting on their own. They are used as instruments,3 and above all, they are victims. A case in point from the Americas is Fidel Castro’s Cuba orchestrating migration crises—the Mariel crisis in 1980 and the rafters (balseros) crisis in 1994—to embarrass various US administrations.4 This difference is not simply terminological. It shapes how governments should respond, which rules apply, and how we judge those involved. Treating weaponized migration as merely a more organized version of ‘regular’ irregular migration leads to the wrong policies. It also makes it harder to identify who is responsible, which is exactly what those actors want. The cases of Belarus, Türkiye, and Morocco offer three variations on the same strategic logic, each exposing a different dimension of Europe’s exposure.

Belarus: The Operation

The 2021 Belarusian case is one of the most thoroughly documented of its kind. After the EU imposed sanctions in response to Alexander Lukashenko’s fraudulent election victory in 2020 and the brutal crackdown on the protests that followed, the regime put together a systematic campaign to push migrants toward the Polish, Lithuanian, and Latvian borders. State-controlled airlines sold what were marketed as tourist packages to people from Iraq, Syria, Yemen, Afghanistan, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo—flights to Minsk, accommodation included, priced at between $2,000 and $4,000, with the tacit agreement that passage into the EU would follow. Border troops then ferried the arrivals to frontier zones in government vehicles, cut through existing fencing, and handed out tools for forcing crossings. Night-vision footage from October and November of that year caught the operation in unusual detail.5

At least 21 migrants died in the forests along the Polish border, and this figure almost certainly fails to cover all fatalities, given that aid organizations and independent media were barred from the restricted zones.6 The dead were not collateral damage in an ordinary humanitarian emergency. They were collateral damage in a hybrid military operation—one whose designers, safe and warm in Minsk, had correctly calculated that the operation’s non-military character would paralyse the EU’s response. Calls to invoke Article 4 of the NATO Treaty, which provides for consultation when a member’s territorial integrity is threatened, were floated but came to nothing. The doctrinal frameworks simply did not fit.

‘Migration is being used as a weapon’

Poland did what it could: it sent troops, passed emergency laws, and built a steel barrier over five metres high that cost more than €400 million. The European Commission, human rights groups, and European courts all criticised these actions. Some of this criticism was fair, since conditions at the border were harsh and legal rules were not always followed. But the debate was unbalanced. Warsaw was judged by laws meant for peacetime humanitarian situations, while Minsk faced no similar scrutiny. That imbalance was intentional. It was the central pillar of the strategy.

Türkiye: The Deal and Its Discontents

The Turkish case is structurally different, and in some respects more troubling because it reveals how Europe itself constructed the leverage that was later used against it. The 2016 EU–Türkiye Statement committed Ankara to preventing irregular departures from Turkish territory in exchange for €6 billion in financial support, visa liberalization dialogue, and the revival of accession talks.7 The arrangement worked, after a fashion: Aegean crossings fell sharply in the months following the agreement. But it also created a durable mechanism of dependency. EU border control had been subcontracted to a non-member state with its own interests, ambitions, and its own reading of the bargain.

‘Europe has no policy for dealing with state-driven migration as a form of hybrid pressure’

Erdoğan’s announcement in March 2020 did not mean the deal had collapsed. Instead, it showed what the deal really was: a signal that Türkiye could open the border as easily as it could close it, and that Ankara, not Brussels, would set the price for keeping it shut. The timing was deliberate, since tensions over Idlib and the Eastern Mediterranean were high. For Türkiye, migration is not simply a problem to manage—it is a tool. Europe gave this tool its value with the 2016 agreement and has been paying for it ever since.

Spain and Morocco: Capitulation Through Managed Migration

The Spanish case is the third—and perhaps the clearest—example of migration being used as a tool of pressure, and succeeding. In May 2021, after Madrid agreed to provide medical treatment to Brahim Ghali, the leader of the Polisario Front, Morocco largely stopped enforcing the border near Ceuta, Spain’s exclave in North Africa. Rabat saw Spain’s decision as a political challenge and responded quickly. In about two days, around 10,000 people, including many unaccompanied minors, crossed into Spain. Moroccan officials did not hide what was happening or why. This was not a border failure or a sudden surge. It was a clear message.

What happened in Madrid in the following months was striking. In March 2022, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez supported Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara, breaking with more than 70 years of Spanish policy. No one in the Spanish government officially linked this change to the events in Ceuta, but the timing is hard to ignore. After seeing thousands cross its border in just two days, Spain changed its position on a major foreign policy issue. The pressure was effective.

The wider migration dynamic between Spain and Morocco points to a more structural factor. The geography of irregular migration into Spain is not simply the product of economic conditions or individual decisions made by people on the move. The distribution of flows—across the Western Mediterranean, the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands, and the land borders at the North African exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla—closely tracks the degree of cooperation Moroccan authorities decide to extend at any given moment.

The dramatic changes observed in recent years are difficult to explain otherwise. During 2024, arrivals to the Canary Islands surged to record levels as the Atlantic route became the principal gateway into Spain. Yet in 2025, arrivals to the archipelago fell by approximately 62 per cent, dropping from nearly 47,000 to fewer than 18,000 migrants. Spanish authorities credited the decline largely to boosted migration-control cooperation involving Morocco, Mauritania, and Senegal. At the same time, however, irregular arrivals increased by 24.5 per cent in the Balearic Islands, while entries into Ceuta and Melilla rose by almost 44 per cent. Overall, irregular arrivals to Spain fell from 64,019 in 2024 to 36,775 in 2025, a 42.6 per cent reduction.8 Yet the decline was accompanied by a striking geographical redistribution of pressure, rather than its elimination.

The significance of this shift should not be underestimated. Unlike the Atlantic route, where departures depend on a chain of transit countries stretching across West Africa and the Sahel, irregular entries into Ceuta and Melilla are almost entirely dependent on decisions made in Rabat. Every person attempting to cross the fences, approach the border infrastructure, or reach Spanish territory through the enclaves must first be allowed to reach the border from inside Morocco. As a result, fluctuations in arrivals at Ceuta and Melilla are probably the clearest available indicator of Morocco’s willingness to manage migration pressure. When Moroccan authorities decide to enforce controls seriously, crossings drop to negligible levels. When enforcement is loosened, figures rise quickly. The events of May 2021 made this reality hard to dispute.

The same logic applies to the Atlantic route, though less directly. Migrants travelling from Mali, Senegal, Guinea, and other West African countries do not wash up on the shores of the Canary Islands by chance. They first have to move through a long corridor running through Mauritania and, in many cases, Moroccan territory or areas under Moroccan influence, before reaching any departure point. The sharp drop in arrivals to the Canary Islands in 2025, following renewed cooperation agreements with Morocco, Mauritania, and Senegal, illustrates that the route does not simply respond to autonomous migratory forces. It expands when transit states are willing to let movement through, and contracts when they are not. In practice, Rabat exerts considerable influence over whether migrants are allowed to continue northward toward embarkation points or are stopped before they reach them.

‘Whether migration should be treated primarily as a humanitarian issue or as a matter of sovereignty and national security must also be addressed’

This shows that migration management is primarily political,9 not just a humanitarian or demographic issue. Morocco can not only increase or decrease migration pressure on Spain, but also shift it to different places. Pressure can focus on the Canary Islands, move to the Western Mediterranean, or go through Ceuta and Melilla, depending on Morocco’s diplomatic goals and how much it wants to cooperate. Migration is not simply a shared problem—it is a tool that can be adjusted to fit wider political aims.

Spain’s internal response has worsened this weakness. Disputes between Madrid and the autonomous regions, especially over how to handle unaccompanied minors, show that Spain struggles to deal with outside pressure. Legal battles like the Aragón case over migrant distribution show how migration crises quickly turn into domestic political fights. This creates a cycle: Morocco takes advantage of Spain’s divided institutions, and Spain’s internal disagreements make Morocco’s pressure more effective.

Unlike in Italy, where migration has mostly been used as a threat, Spain shows how ongoing managed migration can lead to real foreign policy changes and long-term dependence on a neighbour’s cooperation. The 2022 policy shift on Western Sahara, along with Morocco’s ongoing control over migration routes, suggests that Spain is not just vulnerable to migration pressure, but now explicitly relies on Morocco’s restraint. This makes Spain one of the clearest examples in Europe of diplomacy formed by the deliberate use of migration.

The Structural Asymmetry

These three cases share a common pattern. There are few limits to the uses authoritarian countries can make of migration as a weapon. Their leaders make decisions centrally, face few legal restrictions, and do not worry much about their reputations. Lukashenko’s regime ignored criticism from European courts. Morocco did not consider ethics before easing border controls at Ceuta. Erdoğan did not check whether his actions fit with EU asylum law.

Liberal democracies face pressures that their rivals do not. They must follow international refugee law and the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Their institutions are divided at many levels. Any tough response brings political risks at home. They also work hard to appear humane. These are not weaknesses—in most cases, they are real strengths. But they become vulnerable when others create situations meant to take advantage of them.

Hungary’s experience is important to consider. During the 2015 migration crisis, Budapest was among the first to say that large-scale irregular migration was not merely a humanitarian issue but also about sovereignty, border security, and state capacity. Most debates focused on Hungary’s tone and language, not on its main point: that controlling migration can give outside actors geopolitical power. Ten years later, the cases of Belarus, Türkiye, and Morocco show this was a real vulnerability, not just an ideological concern. European legislators now find it harder to ignore.

Hannah Arendt wrote that a stateless person is deprived not just of citizenship but of ‘the right to have rights’—that human rights, however universally proclaimed, require a political community capable of guaranteeing them.10 This means that if a society cannot keep its own political community together, it cannot guarantee rights to anyone, even those it wants to help. If Europe gives up control of its borders, it does not become more humane. Instead, it becomes a stage for other countries’ coercive actions, with real people caught in the middle.

The Gap in the Framework

The 2023 EU Pact on Migration and Asylum represents a genuine effort to systematize Europe’s approach to irregular migration.11 Screening procedures, accelerated border processing, and a solidarity mechanism between member states are meaningful reforms. But the Pact contains a critical blind spot: it treats all irregular arrivals under essentially the same legal and procedural framework, regardless of whether their movement was spontaneous, facilitated, or deliberately orchestrated by a hostile state. It has no category for weaponization.

This gap is not merely administrative. It reflects a deeper reluctance—in Brussels, in national capitals, and in the legal culture of European institutions—to even acknowledge that migration can function as an instrument of coercion. To do so would require treating the question as one of security as well as humanitarianism, and would necessitate the development of attribution and response mechanisms that resemble those used in hybrid-warfare doctrine; it would, in short, require thinking about migration in terms that European liberal politics has spent decades actively resisting.

Lithuania’s emergency legislative response to the Belarusian operation—expedited procedures, military deployment, measures subsequently examined and substantially validated by the European Commission as proportionate—suggests that the gap can be partially closed through legislative innovation when the political will exists. The operative condition is the last one.

What Is to Be Done

The core problem is clear: Europe has no policy for dealing with state-driven migration as a form of hybrid pressure. There are no agreed-upon rules for identifying which state is behind such actions. There is no legal or systematic way to distinguish between spontaneous and engineered migration. The current legal system, built for peacetime humanitarian needs, often punishes frontline states for doing what the situation demands.

This does not mean giving up the ideals that define Europe. It means creating institutions and laws that still work even when those values are being used against Europe. Recognizing that authoritarian governments can create mass asylum claims for their own goals does not weaken the right to asylum. Humanitarian duties do not vanish just because they can be used as pressure. The goal is to build systems that can tell the difference and respond appropriately.

At a minimum, that means several things. A formal doctrine for identifying and responding to state-directed migration as a hybrid threat, developed through the European External Action Service (EEAS). At the very least, this requires a few steps. Europe needs a formal policy for identifying and responding to state-driven migration as a hybrid threat, developed in coordination with the EEAS, Frontex, and national intelligence agencies. EU migration laws should recognize coerced migration as a separate category. Agreements like the EU–Türkiye deal need stronger checks and balances, since the existing setup gives Ankara too much leverage. Member states also need better coordination across all levels of government, since outside pressure often targets weak spots. Whether migration should be treated primarily as a humanitarian issue or as a matter of sovereignty and national security must also be addressed. Whatever one’s assessment of the policies pursued by successive Hungarian governments, the wider European experience has gradually blurred the distinction between these two categories. The cases examined here demonstrate that migration can be instrumentalized by foreign governments to pursue strategic objectives.

Hungary’s main challenge in the coming years is not whether migration will continue to be an important issue in politics, but how future governments will handle it. It is unclear whether the new Hungarian government will continue to focus on border control and resisting migration pressure or choose a different path. If it changes course, it will probably be to please Brussels rather than because of strong support from Hungarian voters. After all, Orbán’s migration policy remained popular in Hungary, even after years of EU sanctions and legal battles that affected citizens.

In the end, Hungary’s debate is just one example of a bigger European issue. The reforms suggested here are not extreme or impossible. They mostly require political will, not major institutional changes. The real question is whether Europe’s leaders can openly admit what is happening: that migration is being used as a weapon, that this is a form of aggression, and that responding to it does not mean giving up humanitarian values. Until leaders can say this clearly, borders will remain open to those who know how to exploit them.

2 Joseph S. Nye, Soft Power: The Means to Success in World Politics (PublicAffairs, 2004).

3 Éva Eszter Szabó, ‘Migration as a Tool of U.S. Foreign Policy in the Cold War’, Hungarian Review, 8/3 (May 2017), 75–88. www.hungarianreview.com/article/20170517_migration_as_a_tool_of_us_foreign_policy_in_the_cold_war.

name: Human Rights
title: El Salvador Faces a Homeland Crisis as TPS Ends for Thousands Abroad
description:
For many, El Salvador is less a homeland than a country inherited through documents, stories, and fear.
Her mother obtained Temporary Protected Status for both of them after El Salvador was designated for the program in 2001.
She has no memories of El Salvador.
El Salvador has spent generations exporting people.
El Salvador may be written on their birth certificates.
text:
More than 170,000 Salvadorans in the United States could lose legal protection on September 9, turning a bureaucratic deadline into a family rupture. For many, El Salvador is less a homeland than a country inherited through documents, stories, and fear.

When Temporary Status Becomes a Lifetime

Alma remembers being lifted onto a chair so immigration officers could take her fingerprints.

She was little enough to think it was a game.

Only years later did she understand what was happening. The officers were collecting biometric information for the immigration protection that would shape nearly every year of her life in the United States.

“I grew up with TPS,” Alma, now 30 and living in Missouri, told EFE. She asked that her last name not be published because she fears retaliation.

She arrived in the United States when she was 18 months old. Her mother obtained Temporary Protected Status for both of them after El Salvador was designated for the program in 2001. Alma went to school in America, bought a house, built a career and became a supervisor at the company where she works.

She has no memories of El Salvador.

Yet on September 9, the legal status that allowed her to construct that life is scheduled to expire.

“I grew up with an American life, with American values,” she told EFE. “Why do they want to take us out?”

Her question exposes the strange contradiction at the heart of TPS. The program was created as temporary protection, but temporary can acquire an entirely different meaning when it lasts a quarter-century.

A five-year-old becomes 30. Workers become supervisors. Renters sign mortgages. Children are born. Parents die.

The immigration category remains temporary even when the human life built beneath it becomes permanent.

For approximately 170,000 Salvadorans, according to figures cited by the National Immigration Forum, expiration means losing work authorization and legal permission to remain in the United States. For some, old deportation orders suspended while they held TPS could become active again.

The word officials may use is return.

For Alma, it does not feel like one.

“When people tell me, ‘go back’ to El Salvador, for me it isn’t going back to a life because I didn’t live there,” she told EFE.

That distinction is more than emotional. It is the central difficulty of treating migration as though geography alone determines belonging.

José Palma has spent years living with the same uncertainty.

The 48-year-old coordinator of the TPS Alliance, a coalition formed in 2017 to advocate for permanent legal status, is the father of four U.S. citizens. He told EFE that the approaching deadline has already changed how his family lives.

A construction project at his house has been stopped. Spending has been cut. Money is being saved for whatever comes next.

TPS holders have learned to live with documents that must be renewed and futures that cannot quite be guaranteed.

“We would have applied a long time ago,” Palma told EFE of permanent residency. “Who wants to live without knowing what will happen with their future?”

That question becomes harder after 25 years.

Many Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries have become deeply integrated into local economies. Migration and human rights expert Celia Medrano told EFE that many have lived legally in the United States for more than two decades, speak English, hold jobs, pay taxes, own homes or carry mortgages and have their immediate families around them.

She estimated typical annual incomes among beneficiaries at between $40,000 and $50,000.

Those details matter because deportation is usually imagined as the movement of an individual across a border.

In reality, it can dismantle an economic unit.

Alma’s employer in Missouri is preparing to lose workers who have been there for years, some since 2001. Their jobs will eventually be filled. The factory will continue operating.

That continuity troubles her.

“It hurts to see how life will keep flowing and they will be replaced,” she told EFE, while the people losing TPS leave “with nothing.”

There is another population hidden behind the 170,000 adults.

Medrano estimates that roughly 150,000 children and adolescents whose Salvadoran parents hold TPS could be affected. Many were born in the United States and are American citizens.

The expiration of one parent’s immigration status can therefore create choices no child made: separation from a mother or father, relocation to a country the child may never have visited, or a divided household stretched across borders.

Migration statistics rarely capture that geometry.

One deportation can create several forms of displacement at once.

Returning to a Country That Has Changed

El Salvador itself presents another complication.

The country to which TPS holders may be sent is not necessarily the country they left.

Medrano warned that reintegration could be difficult because beneficiaries have built economic and social lives under very different conditions. She told EFE that returning Salvadorans may encounter high unemployment, rising poverty and a labor market in which more than 60 percent of the economically active population works in the informal sector.

For someone who has spent 20 or 25 years earning a U.S. salary, maintaining a mortgage and working inside a formal employment system, that adjustment is not simply cultural.

It is structural.

A person can speak Spanish, carry a Salvadoran passport and still arrive as something close to a stranger.

That is the deeper paradox facing the country.

El Salvador has spent generations exporting people. Migration became an economic survival strategy for families and, through remittances, an important pillar of national life. Yet the possibility of mass forced return raises questions about whether the country can absorb people whose skills, expectations, children and financial obligations were formed elsewhere.

Medrano argues the Salvadoran government should prepare for that possibility now.

There is also the question of civic reintegration. She warned that many Salvadorans remain reluctant to express political opinions publicly for fear of consequences, a climate that could feel unfamiliar to returnees accustomed to different forms of political participation in the United States.

None of this means TPS was intended to last forever.

That is precisely the problem.

Successive American governments allowed a temporary humanitarian program to become the legal foundation for entire adult lives without creating a durable solution for many of the people living under it.

Alma’s mother waited for one.

She died before it came.

Now her daughter is still waiting.

The September 9 deadline will be described in official language as the expiration of a migration benefit. For Alma, Palma and thousands of families, the experience will be less administrative.

It will be a test of what the word home actually means after 25 years.

El Salvador may be written on their birth certificates.

But America is where many learned to read them.

text:
Conditions in the Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s rapidly expanding detention center network are appalling and must be corrected before we become the kind of tyranny America was founded to overthrow.

A recent report from Physicians for Human Rights suggests that, in the worst tradition of authoritarian states, ICE is depriving detainees of medical care and showing callous disregard for human life.

The report documents an increase in death rates in ICE custody during the second Trump administration. In the first 12 months of this administration, 39 detainees died in custody, the most of any 12-month period since ICE was formed in 2003. Some of these people were peaceful, longtime residents picked up during roundups. Now they are dead, and their families, in some cases, have not received an explanation.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It’s not just the raw number of deaths that’s disturbing. The rate of deaths in ICE custody has also increased, according to the report. As of January 2026, the rate of death on a monthly basis in the second Trump administration was about 8.4 per 10,000. That’s almost twice the rate of the previous peak, at the height of the COVID-19 outbreak in 2020, and the largest single-year increase on record.

“Although the detained population has grown in recent months, the number of deaths has increased at a disproportionately higher rate, indicating that increased detention alone does not account for the rise in mortality,” the report said.

Physicians for Human Rights, which comprises doctors, public health researchers, lawyers and administrators, won the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize for its work on land mines. The group also helped expose torture at CIA black sites during the war on terror after the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. Now, the group is blowing the whistle on ICE’s disregard for international law and its own rules, and calling for the agency to address the rising death rates.

A review of autopsy reports and other available information on the 39 deceased individuals suggests that ICE did not provide adequate medical care in most cases. ICE also flouted its own policies by failing to investigate the deaths and provide families a timely and thorough explanation, according to the report. Family and detainee interviews were conducted by the group’s partners at another nonprofit, Human Rights Watch.

Some of the deaths might have been prevented, the report found. Those include a detainee who complained of breathing difficulties but received no medical care until he was found unresponsive; people whose high blood pressure was not monitored; individuals with obvious sepsis risk factors who did not have blood cultures drawn despite developing high fevers; and delays in CPR for unresponsive individuals.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Specific cases are chilling: Maksym Chernyak, a 44-year-old man who escaped the war in Ukraine died after suffering a stroke in a Miami facility in early 2025. “Delays in getting [Chernyak] to higher level medical care almost certainly contributed to his death,” according to the report.

In September 2025, Ismael Ayala-Uribe, a 39-year-old Mexican citizen, died in a California detention center from what doctors at the nonprofit said was likely septic shock. “His repeated attempts to obtain appropriate medical help for an infected abscess were recurrently mishandled,” according to the report.

Certain ICE facilities have become notorious for deaths and allegations of medical neglect. Three detainees housed in Delaney Hall in New Jersey have died since December. Detainees at the facility, reopened by the Trump administration in 2025, have told the press about unsanitary conditions and insufficient medical care.

The American Civil Liberties Union is backing a lawsuit filed by former detainees at Camp East Montana near El Paso, the largest detention center by capacity, alleging systematic use of excessive force and withholding of medical care.

The Physicians for Human Rights researchers found the investigations into these deaths were often delayed and cursory.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

I tried to contact ICE about these concerns but did not receive a response. And when administration does release information, it is riddled with political dog whistles and slanted and often inaccurate language. Detainees aren’t “accused” or “suspected” or “detained.” They are “illegal aliens.”

Is this the America that has called out China and Russia for abusing marginal populations and dissidents in their prisons? Is this the America that went to fight tyrannies in Europe in 1941? Is this the America that was birthed in revolt against the authoritarian policies of Britain?

Yes, the border was overwhelmed during the previous Biden administration. And yes, undocumented crossings have slowed under President Donald Trump. But at what cost?

text:
A US federal appeals court on Friday refused to lift a lower court order blocking the Trump administration from using a federal immigration database to verify citizenship information on state voter rolls.

The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled 2-1 against the administration’s request to regain access to the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database.

The lower court had barred the government from using the system ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, when Republicans are seeking to defend their narrow majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate.

Chief Judge Sri Srinivasan and Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, both appointed by former President Barack Obama, upheld the earlier ruling. They found that the use of SAVE in this manner violated the Social Security Act because it involved the sharing of personal information belonging to millions of Americans.

The judges also raised concerns about errors in citizenship records. They warned that inaccurate information could force eligible citizens to provide additional proof of their citizenship to remain registered, while in some cases potentially resulting in their voter registrations being cancelled.

Circuit Judge Gregory Katsas, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, dissented from the decision.

The dispute over the database is part of a broader Republican effort to strengthen citizenship verification in voter registration, while Democrats and voting-rights advocates have raised concerns that such measures could incorrectly remove eligible voters from registration lists.

The legal battle has produced conflicting rulings in different federal courts. In July, a federal judge in Florida ordered the Department of Homeland Security to restore access to the SAVE database for four Republican-led states, after another judge had previously blocked its use nationwide.

The latest appeals court ruling leaves the lower court’s restrictions in place while the wider legal dispute over the federal database and voter-roll checks continues.

text:
NEWPORT, Maine —

Maine State Representative Mike Soboleski, R-Phillips, says a new facility for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will open soon in Newport.

In a post on Facebook on Thursday, Soboleski said construction will soon be underway at the former district courthouse in Newport, saying it "will help the deportation process move even faster."

He shared the information after he said he was part of a group of state lawmakers who conducted an oversight visit to the ICE facility in Scarborough.

"After today's visit I can say for a fact... the illegals in custody are treated with respect, it's clean, food and water are plentiful, and the holding units are large and well lit with private lavatories. A gentleman who was apprehended at 9am was expected to be moved out of state by 1 pm. Apprehended and out of the state in 4-5 hours. That is what I voted for! Great work ICE," he wrote.

The District Court in Newport closed in January of 2025 due to mold.

Maine's Total Coverage reached out to ICE to confirm the plans for a facility in Newport. A spokesperson said the agency would not confirm office locations "as our officers are facing a coordinated campaign of violence against them including an 8,000% increase in death threats against them and a 1,300% increase in assaults against them."

The spokesperson, who did not provide their name, then questioned why we were even asking about the reported plans.

“Is it really news that when a federal agency hires more personnel that they need more space? Thanks to the Big Beautiful Bill, we have an additional 12,000 ICE officers and agents on the ground across the country. That’s a 120% increase in our workforce,” the spokesperson said.

In August, Maine's Total Coverage reported that the number of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) employees in Maine is on the rise, according to federal workforce data.

During the last decade, ICE had an average of 34 employees working in Maine. That number is up to 52, which is a 44% jump from last year, according to data from the U.S. Office of Personnel Management.
