title: Statement of changes HC 584: sponsorship rules eased for modern slavery victims and ...
description:
The latest statement of changes to the immigration rules has been published, accompanied by an explanatory memorandum and a ministerial statement.
Skilled Worker visa holders can leave their abusive sponsor A Skilled Worker’s immigration status is tied to their sponsoring employer.
The explanatory memorandum states that the aim is to encourage victims to come forward early and to reduce the scope for sponsors to use immigration status as a means of control.
A new route will also open under the Government Authorised Exchange scheme for supernumerary work placements and internships linked to Erasmus+.
The rules now reflect this and such children can keep their pre-settled status and go on to qualify for settled status.
text:
The latest statement of changes to the immigration rules has been published, accompanied by an explanatory memorandum and a ministerial statement. If you want to see the rules in context, we have updated our Free Movement immigration rules browser app and you can move the date slider forward to the upcoming commencement dates so that you can see what the rules will be from then.

Skilled worker visa holders who are recognised as victims of modern slavery will no longer be tied to their exploitative sponsor, and the visitor and student routes are being adapted to accommodate the UK’s return to the Erasmus+ programme. Plus a number of other changes set out below.

Unless stated otherwise, the changes take effect on 8 October 2026.

Part Suitability breach of immigration laws extended

A new SUI 11.4(e) is added to Part Suitability so that an applicant is also treated as having been in breach of immigration laws if they have previously acted to frustrate immigration controls as set out in SUI 11.7. This discretionary ground of refusal only previously applied to those applying for entry and it is being extended to those applying for leave within the country as well now.

The explanatory memorandum states that this is intended to cover applicants who have previously failed to report in accordance with their bail conditions, or who have absconded from bail or custody.

Skilled Worker visa holders can leave their abusive sponsor

A Skilled Worker’s immigration status is tied to their sponsoring employer. If they experience exploitation and leave their employer, they generally have a limited period of time to find a new sponsor before their permission is cancelled. This can leave workers stuck in exploitative working conditions, since raising a complaint could put their status at risk.

To address this, SW 18.3 is inserted to Appendix Skilled Worker:

SW 18.3. A Skilled Worker who has been referred into the National Referral Mechanism and is in receipt of a positive Conclusive Grounds decision, where that decision was made during their most recent permission, may have the conditions in SW 18.2(b) to (e) amended, such that any work (including self-employment and voluntary work) is permitted, except for work as a professional sportsperson (including as a sports coach).

A Skilled Worker who has been referred into the National Referral Mechanism and receives a positive conclusive grounds decision will no longer be restricted by the usual work restrictions. They may work for any employer, including on a self-employed or voluntary basis, for the remainder of their visa. The exception is that they cannot take on work as a professional sportsperson or sports coach, which remains prohibited.

The explanatory memorandum states that the aim is to encourage victims to come forward early and to reduce the scope for sponsors to use immigration status as a means of control. The effectiveness of the change will depend on how many workers are actually identified as victims in the first place. It is increasingly difficult to be recognised as a victim of modern slavery, and not everyone subjected to abuse fits the narrow definition. As Dr Dora-Olivia Vicol from Work Rights Centre put it:

The threshold for modern slavery recognition is high, and current definitions routinely fail to protect workers subjected to wage theft or recruitment fee fraud. If officials continue to turn away victims of financial scams and severe labour abuses, this new freedom will remain out of reach for the vast majority who need it.

There was a massive backlog of trafficking cases but that had fallen at the time of our last write up on this in May, with waiting times for a conclusive grounds decision down from over two years in 2024 to 53 days by March 2026. It seems likely that this change will cause an increase in referrals. Let’s hope the Home Office has thought ahead and will resource the trafficking teams properly.

Fee removed for human rights claims in the Family Returns Process

Families in the Family Returns Process, meaning families with children who are due to be removed from the UK, will be able to raise an Article 8 private or family life claim directly with Home Office staff, without making a formal application, paying a fee or using a specified form.

This brings the position for families in line with that already applying to people in immigration detention. The Home Office states that this reflects existing practice, and the rule change provides a legal basis for it.

Fee waiver request application date

Paragraph 34G(4), which sets the date of application following a fee waiver request, is amended to confirm that the application submitted after a fee waiver decision must be for the route specified in the fee waiver request itself.

The explanatory memorandum states this is aimed at applicants (presumably Skilled Worker visa holders) who make a human rights application to extend their permission under section 3C of the Immigration Act 1971, then vary it to a non-human rights application afterwards.

Variation applications and biometric enrolment

Paragraph 34BB(2A) is inserted which confirms that where an application is varied, the applicant must enrol their biometrics within the period set for the original application. This reflects existing policy under the Immigration (Biometric Registration) Regulations 2008, which has not previously appeared in the Immigration Rules themselves.

The explanatory memorandum states this is aimed at applicants who make repeated variations to a human rights application without enrolling biometrics for any of them, again in the context of extending permission under section 3C.

Victim of domestic abuse route extended to adult children

Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse covered partners and their children whose relationship had broken down because of abuse. It is being extended to adult dependent children whose relationship has broken down with their parent that they are dependent on for permission to remain in the UK, for the same reasons.

VDA 4.2 will now read as follows:

VDA 4.2. The applicant must meet one of the following requirements:

(a) The relationship between the applicant and their partner must have broken down permanently as a result of domestic abuse; or

(b) The relationship between the applicant and their parent or parent’s partner must have broken down permanently as a result of domestic abuse.

This follows a Northern Ireland High Court order, JR337’s Application for Judicial Review [2026] NIKB 12, which found the Migrant Victims of Domestic Abuse Concession unlawful as applied to an adult child dependent on her parent for her immigration status. The Home Office has accepted that continuing to exclude adult children from the settlement route would likely lead to further successful challenges, and that dependent parents are in an analogous position.

The change is only expected to result in between 163 and 447 additional grants a year.

Visitor and Student route changes for Erasmus+ programme

The UK agreed to rejoin the Erasmus+ programme as part of the UK-EU Common Understanding package agreed in May 2025. This statement makes the rule changes needed to accommodate that.

Under Appendix Visitor, UK state schools and academies will be able to host Erasmus+ participants for study placements of up to six months. Changes to Appendix Visitor: Permitted Activities mean all visitors will be allowed to attend workshops, debates and skills competitions. Erasmus+ participants will also be able to take courses, receive or give training, undertake traineeships and, for sports organisations, undertake coaching and training assignments.

The Student and Child Student routes are amended so Erasmus+ participants can study at RQF level 2 and above (SCQF level 5 and above in Scotland) without needing to work towards an approved qualification.

Where an Erasmus+ course includes a work placement, the sponsor rules are relaxed. State schools and academies will also become eligible to hold student sponsor licences so they can sponsor Erasmus+ students.

A new route will also open under the Government Authorised Exchange scheme for supernumerary work placements and internships linked to Erasmus+.

Changes to the EU Settlement Scheme

Several changes are being made to the EU Settlement Scheme. Pre-settled status will no longer be automatically lost where someone stops meeting the eligibility requirements but removing their status would be disproportionate, for example following a sudden change in family circumstances.

The deadline for a first-time joining family member to apply is now three months from their most recent lawful entry to the UK since the end of the transition period, which better reflects the Withdrawal Agreement. The EUSS travel permit route which allowed settlement scheme holders to travel back to the UK on a new passport is being removed. The ‘Update My Details’ service should be used instead.

Another change is in response to the Ayoola v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2025] EWCA Civ 1519 judgment. This was where the Court of Appeal held that a child with pre-settled status, whose EU citizen parent was formerly a worker or self-employed person in the UK, retains a right of residence under the Withdrawal Agreement until they complete their education here. This is even after they cease to qualify as a family member. The rules now reflect this and such children can keep their pre-settled status and go on to qualify for settled status. Their primary carer, along with any dependant under 18, may do the same where necessary for the child’s education in the UK to continue.

These changes take effect on 8 October 2026. A separate change removing the option to prove identity using an expired biometric residence permit, since almost all such permits had already expired by the end of 2024, takes effect later, on 9 December 2026.

Settlement requirement for BN(O) children

Dependent children on the Hong Kong British National (Overseas) route had to complete a five-year period of continuous residence before they could settle, separately from their parents. This requirement is being removed so children can settle alongside a parent who meets the settlement requirements, bringing the route into line with the approach taken under most other immigration categories.

HK 62.1 will now read:

The applicant must meet the following requirements:

(a) the applicant’s most recent grant of permission must have been on the Hong Kong BN(O) route; and,

(b) the applicant must have spent a continuous period of 5 years with permission in the UK on a route under which a person can settle, unless they are aged under 18 at the date of application.

Other minor changes

Visitors will no longer need to show that training they want to undertake in the UK is unavailable in their home country, and artists, entertainers, and musicians will be allowed to attend rehearsals under the Visitor route. Entertainment staff will also be able to assist with activities permitted under PA.14.1, and a new definition of entertainment staff supporting a performer is added.

The Tier 1 (Entrepreneur) and Tier 1 (Investor) provisions relating to entry clearance and extension applications that can no longer be made have been removed, as has the Start-up route.

Appendix Child Relative (Sponsors with Protection) is amended so decision makers can reject an entry clearance application from an applicant who is over 18.

A couple of other small changes take effect later in the year, including on both the T2 Minister of Religion and Appendix Temporary Work – Religious Worker routes, which come into force on 29 October 2026. The student maintenance requirement is increasing in line with the annual uplift, from £1,529 to £1,570 a month outside London and from £1,171 to £1,203 in London. This takes effect on 30 November 2026.

name: Human Rights
title: ICE's new 'shock gloves' are dangerous, inhumane and totally unnecessary - The Hill
authors: Raul A. Reyes, opinion contributor, Raul A. Reyes, opinion contributor
description:
“It’s another device to help someone get compliant when they are not.” These shock gloves are a new low in ICE’s campaign of cruelty.
With the shock gloves, agents will have a new tool with which to inflict pain on anyone they say is suspected of being in the country illegally.
The manufacturer of the shock gloves warns that they should not be used on children, pregnant woman, the elderly or disabled people.
ICE’s shock gloves raise legal issues as well.
ICE’s shock gloves are dangerous, inhumane and unnecessary.
text:
According to a recent Department of Homeland Security notice, the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency plans to spend up to $20 million on gloves that deliver painful electric shocks. At the push of a button, a one-second shock from these gloves can send a grown man to the ground.

On “Fox & Friends,” White House border czar Tom Homan said the gloves would prevent ICE agents from needing to use deadly force. “It’s another device to help someone get compliant when they are not.”

These shock gloves are a new low in ICE’s campaign of cruelty. Their use holds great potential for harm to migrants and U.S. citizens alike, and will enable more ICE brutality while helping agents evade accountability for their actions.

The manufacturer of the gloves, formally named the Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, markets them as a “de-escalation device.” But there is no reason to believe that ICE agents will use them that way. Instead, the gloves will likely embolden a paramilitary force known for aggressive behavior, racial profiling and violence.

ICE agents have kicked, punched and tackled people hundreds of times, and deployed chemical irritants regularly. They use chokeholds and neck restraints, tactics that are prohibited by other law enforcement agencies. They have fatally shot at least three confirmed American citizens: Alex Pretti, Renee Good and Ruben Ray Martinez. With the shock gloves, agents will have a new tool with which to inflict pain on anyone they say is suspected of being in the country illegally.

The manufacturer of the shock gloves warns that they should not be used on children, pregnant woman, the elderly or disabled people. Yet ICE frequently encounters members of these high-risk categories. People with disabilities are especially vulnerable to harm from the gloves, because not all medical conditions — like epilepsy, heart disease or mental health issues — are visible. Given that ICE disproportionately targets Latinos, a demographic with high rates of cardiovascular disease, the planned use of the gloves will almost certainly lead to serious medical incidents.

Consider that the gloves’ training manual comes with a red warning label, noting that improper use may result in injury or death.

The rationale behind the use of such gloves is disturbing. They were specifically designed to be “low optics,” meaning their use will not be visible as other policing methods. On a promotional video by the manufacturer, supporters of the gloves say that they “Look better to those witnesses” and that they are “conducive to not leading to lawsuits.” Because the electric shocks do not leave burns or marks, there is nothing to stop agents from using the gloves repeatedly on a person, or after a person has been subdued. Nor is there anything to prevent multiple agents from shocking a single person simultaneously. What could possibly go wrong?

The real question is why ICE needs these gloves at all. Immigration agents are well equipped with firearms, pepper spray and batons. ICE and the Customs and Border Protection agency plan to spend $144 million in 2025 on guns, ammunition and “less lethal” weapons such as tasers and pepper sprays, according to a February report by Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.). Just weeks later, the administration announced its intent to purchase more than 17,000 tasers for another $220 million. It’s hard to see how agents need another tool in their arsenal when they are already armed to the hilt.

ICE’s shock gloves raise legal issues as well. Their use may violate the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition of “cruel and unusual punishment,” and the constitutional guarantee of due process. New York’s governor and attorney general have both criticized the new gloves, suggesting that their use may run afoul of state and civil rights laws.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said, “ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country.” Yet ICE is generally not going after “criminal illegal aliens.” About 70 percent of people in immigration detention have no criminal convictions at all. ICE is also operating in an environment with little oversight, as the administration has gutted the agency’s internal watchdogs.

Meanwhile, the president’s popularity is cratering, and a majority of American voters disapprove of how ICE is doing its job. Immigration agents should be reined in, not empowered to inflict more suffering on their targets.

ICE’s shock gloves are dangerous, inhumane and unnecessary. A rogue agency that violates human and civil rights does not deserve more weapons.

title: District Court Issues Preliminary Injunction Against Latest Executive Order on Birthright Citizenship
description:
The court says that the citizenship carveouts in the August 2026 EO are well outside of the narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship recognized by the Supreme Court in its June 2026 decision striking down the first birthright citizenship EO.
On August 6, 2026, President Trump signed two Executive Orders concerning citizenship for individuals born in the United States.
One order set forth what the Administration views as exceptions to birthright citizenship.
The decision upheld the U.S. birthright citizenship framework that has been in place for more than 125 years.
The list of individuals identified as not entitled to birthright citizenship under this EO extends well beyond the long-recognized narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship.
text:
On September 2, a federal district court judge in Maryland issued a preliminary injunction temporarily barring the government from denying U.S. citizenship under President Trump’s August 6, 2026 Executive Order (EO) 14418, “Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship.” The recent EO sought to impose additional exceptions to birthright citizenship, including some related to birth tourism and surrogacy, as detailed further below. The district court case, Casa Inc. v. Trump, Docket No. 8:25-cv-00201 (D. Maryland), is one of the class action lawsuits that successfully challenged President Trump’s January 2025 birthright citizenship EO, which was struck down as unconstitutional in June 2026.

In issuing a preliminary injunction against the August 2026 Order, the district court held that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed in their claim that the EO is unconstitutional as applied to the certified class (children who would have been denied citizenship under President Trump’s January 2025 birthright citizenship EO) because the Supreme Court has already held that children in this class are U.S. citizens at birth under the U.S. Constitution. The court says that the citizenship carveouts in the August 2026 EO are well outside of the narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship recognized by the Supreme Court in its June 2026 decision striking down the first birthright citizenship EO.

On August 6, 2026, President Trump signed two Executive Orders concerning citizenship for individuals born in the United States. One order set forth what the Administration views as exceptions to birthright citizenship. A second order directed the Departments of Homeland Security and State to take action to curb so-called birth tourism.

The Executive Orders came weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down a January 2025 presidential order that sought to limit birthright citizenship in a case called Trump v. Barbara. In that case, the Court ruled that children born in the United States – even to parents who are in the country unlawfully or temporarily – are U.S. citizens at birth under the U.S. Constitution, with a narrow exception for children born to certain foreign diplomats. The decision upheld the U.S. birthright citizenship framework that has been in place for more than 125 years.

President Trump’s August 6 birthright citizenship EO identifies certain categories of children born in the United States to foreign national parents whom the government should deem not entitled to birthright citizenship, based on the Trump Administration’s interpretation of historical exceptions to birthright citizenship discussed in Trump v. Barbara.

Under the EO, the following categories of individuals would not be considered U.S. citizens based on birth in the United States if neither of their parents is a U.S. citizen and if:

either parent engages in a commercial transaction to ensure that the person’s mother is present in the United States to give birth;

either parent engages in a commercial transaction with a surrogate present in the United States to give birth;

either parent engaged in any commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship for the individual, or engaged in fraudulent activity to obtain citizenship;

either parent is an “alien enemy,” which the EO defines to include members of designated foreign terrorist organizations and specially designated global terrorists; or

either parent is a foreign government employee, including foreign diplomats, other employees of foreign embassies or consulates, other foreign government employees, and employees of international organizations having international-organization immunity.

The EO further states that this is a non-exhaustive list of individuals not entitled to birthright citizenship.

The EO prohibits federal government agencies from documenting these individuals as U.S. citizens, or from accepting documents issued by state or local governments purporting to recognize U.S. citizenship for these individuals. The Order also requires executive agencies to issue guidance implementing the order within 30 days. The district court’s September 2 preliminary injunction does not bar federal agencies from issuing guidance under the Order.

The list of individuals identified as not entitled to birthright citizenship under this EO extends well beyond the long-recognized narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship. In particular:

As noted above, under longstanding interpretations and practice, only children of certain foreign diplomats having diplomatic immunity do not acquire citizenship by birth in the United States. Children of other foreign government officials have historically been considered U.S. citizens if born in the United States.

The exception from birthright citizenship for children of “alien enemies” referred to in early case law has generally been considered to cover instances where part of the territory of the United States is occupied by a foreign invading army and the child is born in that occupied territory, rather than referring to designated terrorists, members of terrorist organizations, or other foreign nationals designated or deemed to be enemies.

No exception to birthright citizenship has previously been recognized for children born as a result of birth tourism, surrogacy, or illegal activity.

description:
An immigration officer is facing federal charges for making false statements about the shooting of a Venezuelan migrant during the Trump administration’s deportation crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, several outlets reported.

The Hill has reached out to the Justice Department, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and ICE for comment.

text:
An immigration officer is facing federal charges for making false statements about the shooting of a Venezuelan migrant during the Trump administration’s deportation crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, several outlets reported.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer Christian Castro was in custody in Texas on Thursday evening after a federal grand jury indicted Castro on six counts making materially false statements to investigators.

The Hill has reached out to the Justice Department, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and ICE for comment.

Castro also faces state assault charges in Minnesota for shooting and wounding Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year.

The state charges also include falsely reporting a crime after Castro allegedly told his superiors at DHS that Sosa-Celis and other people attacked him with a snow shovel and a broom — claims disproven by video evidence.

The federal charges follow the officer’s release last week after spending 90 days in a Texas county jail. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) refused to sign extradition papers requested by Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) so he could face charges there.

Mary Moriarty, county attorney for Minnesota’s Hennepin County, said in a statement shared with The Hill that Castro had been arrested again in Texas and said she expected the officer would “appear in federal court” there and eventually in Minnesota.

“Despite Gov. Abbott’s best efforts to shield Mr. Castro, we will see him soon,” she added.

Castro is the first federal immigration officer to be prosecuted by the Justice Department for actions related to the Trump administration’s Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota earlier this year.

The massive immigration crackdown effort, in which thousands of federal troops were deployed to the Twin Cities, sparked controversy after immigration officers shot and killed two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

Robin Wolpert, an attorney for Sosa-Celis, told The Associated Press in a statement that the Justice Department “grossly undercharged this case,” following ProPublica’s reporting earlier this week that found department officials reportedly blocked a prosecutor’s push to bring more serious charges against Castro.

“Mr. Sosa Celis wants Mr. Castro to be held fully accountable for his crimes,” Wolpert said, according to the AP.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Minnesota said in a statement Thursday that it will represent Sosa-Celis in his lawsuit against the Trump administration, in which he will seek damages under the Federal Tort Claims Act.

“Today’s indictment is not enough,” the group’s deputy legal director, Catherine Ahlin-Halverson, said in a statement. “Julio was shot by Christian Castro, arrested, and falsely prosecuted.”

“The enormity of what happened to him is so great, and such an egregious violation of his fundamental rights, that he can never be made whole,” she continued. “We must demand that our system do better to hold these federal agents accountable to him, and to all of us, and that is why we are bringing this administrative claim on his behalf.”

Updated at 10:10 a.m. EDT.

title: 'It's inhumane': six ICE deportees held in one of world's most repressive regimes | Africa
description:

Investigations by the US Senate and the Department of Justice (DoJ) concluded he used bribery and extortion to fund a wild spending spree in Equatorial Guinea, and he eventually reached a settlement to avoid trial.
He then travelled to Washington and secured the third-country deportation deal, under which the US would pay his government $7.5m (£5.5m).
“They cannot legally obtain a status there because Equatorial Guinea doesn’t have a legal framework for asylum, so they’re in this limbo,” said Alicante.
“This is happening in Equatorial Guinea, in Eswatini, Sudan, Ghana, Liberia; in so many places where they are sending mostly innocent people who have not committed a crime in the US.
text:
In late August, around 20 people were put on a flight in the US, shackled at the wrists, waist and ankles, and sent to Liberia as part of one of the largest third-country deportation arrangements of Donald Trump’s second term.

Although more than 23,000 people have been sent to 26 countries other than their own since last year, that day saw something that had not happened before: six people refused to get off the plane – and were instead taken to another country.

Four Cubans, one Brazilian and one Cameroonian refused to disembark in the Liberian capital Monrovia on 20 August; some of them were allegedly assaulted by ICE agents, who returned them to the plane and promised they would be taken back to the US.

A few hours later, however, they were dropped off in another African country: Equatorial Guinea, one of the world’s most repressive and corrupt regimes, where armed men took them to a former luxury hotel turned detention centre in the capital, Malabo, where they have been held ever since.

Meredyth Yoon, the litigation director at Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said: “It’s the first time I’ve heard of people being deported to a third country, refusing to disembark, and then being hastily deported on the same flight to a fourth country.”

The lawyer, who is in close contact with the group, said they were put on the flight without agreeing to, or even knowing they were being sent to Liberia, let alone Equatorial Guinea.

She said they are now being held in “horrific conditions of confinement”, unable to leave the hotel or even contact their families, watched by armed guards, with restricted access to food and no access to basic hygiene items or medical care.

Yoon said: “Their families are terrified, deeply concerned about their safety. They haven’t done anything wrong, and they’re being held against their will without knowing what will happen to them.”

Although deportation by the US to a fourth country appears to be unprecedented, nearly 60 other people, mostly Africans from other countries, have been deported directly to Equatorial Guinea since November.

The country remains far behind Mexico, the main destination for third-country deportees, which has received more than 19,000 people, but Equatorial Guinea has received more than any other country in Africa so far. The agreement with Liberia provides for the transfer of up to 1,200 people.

The flights to Equatorial Guinea are part of a deal secured by vice-president Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, known as Teodorín, the son of the dictator Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, the world’s longest-ruling head of state, who has been in power for nearly half a century.

Teodorín, who has faced criminal proceedings in other countries over money laundering and corruption, had been barred from entering the US. In France, he was tried in absentia and convicted of money laundering, embezzlement of public funds and corruption in 2017, with the conviction upheld by an appeals court in 2020.

Investigations by the US Senate and the Department of Justice (DoJ) concluded he used bribery and extortion to fund a wild spending spree in Equatorial Guinea, and he eventually reached a settlement to avoid trial.

However, the US state department granted him a one-month waiver so he could attend the UN general assembly in New York last year.

He then travelled to Washington and secured the third-country deportation deal, under which the US would pay his government $7.5m (£5.5m).

Tutu Alicante, founder and executive director of the Washington-based NGO EG Justice, said: “For Teodorín, as someone who is about to replace his father as president, having the US on his side is much more important than the money.”

Alicante has also been closely following the situation of about 30 deportees currently being held at the Bamy hotel, owned by Mbasogo’s family and which sits inside an isolated, walled compound heavily patrolled by armed soldiers.

“The conditions they’re being held in are inhumane,” said Alicante. “We’re talking about individuals who have not committed a crime in the US, and they’re locked up 24/7 in small rooms, and many have been deprived of food and water for considerably long periods.”

The Guardian exchanged text messages with one of the Cubans who arrived in late August, who said they were “very saddened” and “desperately hoping to draw attention to what is happening to us, in the hope that someone with the power to help will take pity on us”.

He soon stopped responding, however, because guards had confiscated all the phones to prevent the deportees from speaking to media outlets.

Among them is a man with a large ventral hernia who, after resisting landing in Liberia, was allegedly thrown down the aircraft steps by ICE agents. Last week, he told the Spanish newspaper El País he urgently needed reconstructive abdominal surgery but, when he was taken to a hospital in Malabo, was allegedly denied treatment because he had no documents.

“They cannot legally obtain a status there because Equatorial Guinea doesn’t have a legal framework for asylum, so they’re in this limbo,” said Alicante.

The deportees face two options: indefinite detention at the hotel or being sent back to their countries of origin, as has already happened to almost half of those who have arrived since November.

However, according to the monitoring project, Third Country Deportation Watch, many of these individuals had previously been granted withholding of removal by US immigration judges who found that they faced a real risk of persecution, torture or death in their home countries.

Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration is using third-country deportations as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries.

A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security said: “All of these illegal aliens were deported to a safe third country. We are applying the law as written.

“If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them, period. The Trump administration is utilising all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised.”

The governments of Equatorial Guinea and Liberia did not respond to requests for comment.

Last May, UN human rights experts urged Equatorial Guinea to stop sending US deportees back to their home countries, but, as the Guardian has learned, the practice has continued, with at least four Ethiopians sent back to Ethiopia last Wednesday.

“This is happening in Equatorial Guinea, in Eswatini, Sudan, Ghana, Liberia; in so many places where they are sending mostly innocent people who have not committed a crime in the US. This is unconscionable,” said Alicante.

title: Cities as Nodes of Resistance - Just Security
authors: Jill Habig, Yusuke Saito, Jennifer Connet, Skylar Thompson, Just Security, Ambassador Daniel Fried, Stephen Chamberlin, Leanne Lusk
description:
Local opposition to federal immigration policies is multi-faceted, from denying resources and blocking illegal overreach to channeling the moral authority of their residents.
Even though cities are notably absent from the federal Constitution, state constitutions and laws give cities substantial authority to run their own affairs.
Immigration No issue better displays the range of tools available to cities than modern immigration policy.
The cities challenged the federal effort as a violation of the 10th Amendment, which prevents the federal government from commandeering local resources.
Cities have not yet succeeded in changing federal immigration policies writ large.
text:
In February 1854, Anthony Burns, a young man born into slavery in Virginia, secretly boarded a ship bound for Boston to escape. Months later, his arrest by federal officials sparked outrage. After a violent attack failed to rescue him from the courthouse, a judge ordered Burns returned to slavery. Federal soldiers escorted him through the streets as a crowd of 50,000 people protested.

Before the Civil War, Northern cities like Boston impeded the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793. Residents organized through local uprisings, bail funds, and the Underground Railroad to free people arrested for escaping enslavement. When the federal government responded with the much stricter Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 — complete with criminal liability for anyone who obstructed slave catchers — Black and white Bostonians formed a committee to thwart its enforcement. Other cities codified their resistance in Personal Liberty Acts, like Chicago’s 1850 resolution prohibiting local cooperation with the federal law: “[W]e do not … consider it a part of our duty, or the duty of the City Officers of the City of Chicago, to aid or assist in the arrest of fugitives from oppression.”

Over 175 years later, cities’ historic role as hubs of resistance takes on renewed resonance in today’s era of rising authoritarianism in the United States. Take how cities are responding to attacks on immigrant neighbors. Local opposition to federal immigration policies is multi-faceted, from denying resources and blocking illegal overreach to channeling the moral authority of their residents. During the federal occupation of Minneapolis earlier this year, for example, Mayor Jacob Frey and St. Paul Mayor Melvin Carter staged a press conference at a church with the state governor and faith leaders, and over 100 clergy members were later arrested while protesting ICE.

Even though cities are notably absent from the federal Constitution, state constitutions and laws give cities substantial authority to run their own affairs. They can use local policy and spending power to diverge from federal priorities, withhold local cooperation from the federal government, and increase rights beyond federal guarantees. As constitutional scholar Heather Gerken has termed it, they can “dissent by deciding.” Localities can also litigate to challenge federal policies directly and restrain federal control over city power. And they can marshal collective political leadership to rally public opinion against federal actions. Together, these tactics can expose federal vulnerabilities, slow or halt federal execution, and ultimately help expand the definition of who can access full rights and freedoms. Of course, many of these same tactics have already been deployed by cities against these same rights, such as “sanctuary cities for the unborn” and other anti-abortion tactics Professor Kaitlin Ainsworth Caruso has examined at length.

Immigration

No issue better displays the range of tools available to cities than modern immigration policy. Hundreds of localities have passed what are commonly known as “sanctuary” policies, which restrict how and when they collect and share data, lend local police officers’ time and resources, or honor requests from the federal government to hold people in local jails. While the first wave of sanctuary cities began in the 1970s and ’80s, these policies have taken on new significance during the second Trump administration. Echoing the Personal Liberty Acts of the pre-Civil War period, they force the federal government to bear the significant cost of its own policies — especially in time and personnel — by holding back local support.

Despite intense federal pressure, including efforts to withhold federal funding from local governments, local sanctuary policies have withstood legal scrutiny. In California, San Francisco and Santa Clara Counties defeated the first Trump administration’s attempts to “defund” sanctuary cities in 2017. The cities challenged the federal effort as a violation of the 10th Amendment, which prevents the federal government from commandeering local resources. The second Trump administration has ratcheted up that pressure with direct lawsuits against numerous cities, yet every court to consider the issue — including in a case on behalf of 50 cities and counties — has again sided with local jurisdictions’ power to control their resources free from federal coercion.

Cities have also led the way in resisting the second Trump administration’s violent immigration raids. Boston, Chicago, and Seattle issued executive orders in early 2026 to prevent Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from using city-owned property to stage enforcement activities, and to collect evidence to prosecute federal officials who abuse their power.

When the administration threatened National Guard and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) deployments to Chicago in the fall of 2025, Mayor Brandon Johnson rallied local officials and community members to push back. City leaders held know-your-rights trainings with faith, business, and advocacy groups, and prepared city agencies for a variety of litigation options, including suing over violations of federal laws that restrict the federal government’s power to deploy the military for domestic purposes. The city’s initial response, with support from the state, delayed federal deployment by several weeks and gave local leaders more time to prepare. Ultimately, the city and state’s joint litigation challenging the legality of federal military deployment to the region was successful in the Supreme Court, and the administration abandoned the deployment.

When over 3,000 ICE agents descended on Minneapolis, federal officials lamented the “difficult operating environment” for federal immigration agents because of the strength of local organizing and the absence of city support. After the January 2026 federal killings of Renée Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, outcry from elected officials and community leaders across the country mobilized a bipartisan group of senators to deny increased funding to DHS (the agency that houses ICE). That, and the resulting shift in public opinion, caused the administration to pull agents from Minneapolis just one month later.

In a number of other contexts, cities and counties have directly challenged the legality of federal laws and policies in court, calling attention to the harms they would inflict on local governments and their communities. Cook County, Illinois, for example, joined a local immigrant rights group to challenge the first Trump administration’s public charge rule, which would have banned immigrants from accessing many public benefits. Other cities, including New York, San Francisco, and Baltimore, did the same, and all secured court orders preventing the rule from taking effect.

Cities have not yet succeeded in changing federal immigration policies writ large. Yet through collective resistance, they have both made it harder for the federal government to execute the full horrors of its discriminatory deportation agenda and begun to build a public case for more sweeping change in federal law and practice.

Marriage Equality

Cities have long been strongholds of activism for LGBTQ+ rights, from local anti-discrimination ordinances to laws protecting transgender access to bathrooms and other public spaces. But no LGBTQ+ rights issue has been shaped by cities more than the fight for marriage equality. Marriage equality burst onto the national political stage in the 1990s, when the Hawaii Supreme Court ruled that banning same-sex marriage was discriminatory. The backlash, locally and nationally, was swift, including the federal Defense of Marriage Act in 1996 alongside multiple state-level bans.

Then in late 2003, Massachusetts became the first state permanently to legalize marriage equality. Inspired by that ruling — and dismayed by President George W. Bush’s call for a national ban on same-sex marriage — then-San Francisco Mayor Gavin Newsom launched a daring act of government-sanctioned civil disobedience in February 2004. Mayor Newsom instructed his city clerk to begin issuing marriage licenses, concluding that refusing to do so violated California’s constitution. A month-long “Winter of Love” began, when more than 4,000 same-sex couples tied the knot while national news covered the daily court battle to stop them. Cities across the country joined in, from New Paltz, New York and Multnomah County, Oregon, to Asbury Park, New Jersey and Sandoval County, New Mexico.

When the California Supreme Court later nullified the marriage licenses, it invited San Francisco to challenge the constitutionality of the state’s marriage ban directly. After four years of litigation led by the city in coalition with LGBTQ+ rights groups, the state’s Supreme Court legalized marriage equality in 2008.

Later that fall, California voters passed Proposition 8, a state constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage. Two same-sex couples filed a lawsuit against it in federal court, and the San Francisco City Attorney’s Office joined the case on the side of the couples. After trial, Judge Vaughn Walker ruled that Prop 8 was unconstitutional and that forbidding same-sex couples from marrying violated their civil rights under the U.S. Constitution. The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed an appeal of his ruling on standing grounds — a decision that reinstated marriage equality in California and paved the way for nationwide change just a couple of years later.

The fight for marriage equality demonstrates how local jurisdictions can exert significant power. Mayor Newsom’s initial publicity stunt, while unsuccessful in securing immediate rights, had a lasting impact on public opinion. In full view on their television screens, people saw retired women who had been together for decades bring their grandkids to watch them get married; kids with balloons excited to see their parents officially recognized; couples openly weeping at the public recognition of their love. Over the course of a decade, the city wielded all its tools to rally public opinion and courts to overturn a federal regime that oppressed its people.

Abortion

For decades, abortion has been a contentious legal, political, and policy issue. Since Roe v. Wade in 1973, states have driven that national conversation and tested the bounds of the federal right to abortion. The role of local governments has been less well-understood and appreciated when it comes to abortion rights and access to reproductive health care. But especially since the Supreme Court’s 2022 ruling overturning Roe in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, cities have begun to re-deploy a range of tools from the Fugitive Slave Law era.

Oakland, California, declared itself a sanctuary city in 2022 for women seeking abortions, directly borrowing from the immigration and slavery concepts. Dozens of cities have developed or funded resources for people seeking to travel to abortion care across county and state lines.

Throughout the country, nearly 90 local prosecutors publicly committed not to prosecute abortion cases, blunting the impact of state criminal bans in jurisdictions representing more than 28 million Americans. And several cities have passed versions of the Guarding the Right to Abortion Care for Everyone (Grace) Act, a law instructing local police departments to de-prioritize investigating and prosecuting reproductive healthcare cases.

When local prosecutors do try to build a case, local officials have refused to turn over data or provide assistance. In early 2025, then-Acting Ulster County Clerk Taylor Bruck blocked Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s attempt to file a judgment against a New York doctor who had declined to appear in a Texas lawsuit against her. Bruck’s decision ensured that New York State’s shield law — which aims to prevent hostile states from prosecuting doctors who send medication abortion into their jurisdictions — effectively protected the doctors and patients who depend on them.

Like immigration and the pre-Civil War Personal Liberty Acts, cities are still in a defensive posture on abortion, using their tactics to slow and weaken the tools of criminalization and call attention to the moral outrage of denying care. But for a woman in an apartment in Austin, Texas, who received mifepristone in the mail from a New York doctor, or for a doctor who provided care without fear of prosecution in Tucson, Arizona, local resistance and leadership has offered a safe haven.

* * *

Despite being at the bottom of the national pecking order, cities punch well above their weight and continue to deploy tactics developed in the 1850s to challenge the federal government today. They guard their power, limiting the federal government’s attempts to commandeer their policies and resources. They flex their influence in courts of law and public opinion to expose federal overreach and mobilize communities to fight back. And they band together to secure strength in numbers, reducing the ability of authoritarian regimes to isolate, divide, and conquer. The 21st century federal government has much more power to exact revenge against dissenters. That makes solidarity more important than ever.

text:
At the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, 1.3 million individuals from 17 countries were living and working in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status, or TPS.

TPS is a humanitarian form of protection from deportation for people who cannot return to their home countries because of an armed conflict, environmental disaster or other extraordinary circumstances.

In 2025, the Trump administration began terminating or not renewing TPS for those countries, making its way through 13 of them. As the administration turns its attention to the few remaining nations, most TPS holders have lost or will soon lose their protection from deportation and their authorization to work. Many will be separated from their families and the communities they have lived in for decades. Some will be forced to return to countries like Afghanistan, Haiti and Syria, all of which are on the U.S. State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list due to war, terrorism or other extreme violence.

As a law scholar who studies immigration detention, I can say that most people with TPS never had a path to anything more permanent, which means, as they face deportation, they have little recourse.

Challenges in court

In the fall of 2025, the Trump White House announced that it would not renew Syrian or Haitian TPS; Syria’s would expire in 60 days, Haiti’s in February 2026. Lower courts blocked both terminations, triggering appeals that took the cases to the Supreme Court.

In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled that federal courts cannot review most challenges to a TPS termination because, in the original 1990 law creating TPS, Congress barred judicial review of the decision to give a country TPS – or extend or end it.

James Percival, the general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, celebrated the decision, saying “Temporary Protected Status was always supposed to be temporary and can be canceled at the appropriate time.”

But the ruling means no court can consider whether a cancellation is, in fact, “appropriate,” or whether it follows the law.

Unanswered questions

When Congress passed TPS as part of the Immigration Act of 1990, it was responding to a specific failure: the ad hoc and inconsistent use of something called Extended Voluntary Departure, which permitted a noncitizen to remain in the U.S. regardless of their immigration status.

That discretionary relief allowed some displaced Salvadorans to remain in the U.S. during their country’s civil war in the 1980s, but its application was arbitrary and often discriminatory. Because the U.S. backed the Salvadoran government, Salvadorans were denied both Extended Voluntary Departure and asylum more than 90% of the time – not for lack of merit but because of the government they were fleeing.

Congress recognized a humanitarian need for more uniform protection for people who, like Salvadorans, faced a return to violence or extreme danger but were not covered by narrow asylum laws that require proof of targeted persecution.

A new protected status would “standardize the procedure for granting temporary stays of deportation,” Representative Sander Levin explained at the time.

“Refugees, spawned by the sad and tragic forces of warfare, should not be subject to the vagaries of our domestic politics as well,” Levin added. When the 1990 Immigration Act passed, El Salvador was the first country designated for TPS.

Congress avoided placing time limits on these new TPS designations, leaving that to the discretion of the presidential administration, which would evaluate a country’s humanitarian needs at least every 18 months. Whether TPS holders should ever gain something more permanent was left for future congressional action.

No next step

Not every person from a TPS-designated country is eligible for it. Anything that disqualifies someone from asylum – national security concerns, persecuting others or criminal history – also disqualifies them from TPS.

Congress did not want to incentivize unlawful immigration. For that reason, it wrote the law in such a way that TPS itself could not lead to permanent residence. Lawful permanent residents are eligible to become citizens after five years. TPS recipients, though living in the U.S. lawfully, are not classified as lawful permanent residents.

Congress has since passed laws creating a pathway to permanent residence for certain nationalities, including some with TPS – the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act, for example. It did not do so for most.

TPS designations for some countries have ended after a few years, like Rwanda and Guinea; others have been renewed for decades, like El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua. Over the years, TPS became a kind of limbo status, dependent on each presidential administration’s regular evaluation of a country’s humanitarian conditions – and on Congress to turn TPS into a pathway to lawful permanent residence. For most, the latter never happened.

What happens when TPS ends?

Many people who lose TPS are not eligible for any other immigration status.

Lawful permanent residence, commonly known as a “green card,” is mainly available in three ways: through a close family relationship, like being married to a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident; through a job that requires special skills, like being a professional soccer player; or through asylum status.

Even if a person can apply for permanent residence, their immigration history, such as entering the U.S. without a visa or remaining in the U.S. without lawful status for a certain time, may be a permanent barrier.

TPS holders are given at least 60 days’ notice before termination takes effect, at which point they lose authorization to work and become undocumented, meaning they can be arrested by immigration officers at any time. There is little they can do in those 60 days that would allow them to lawfully remain in the U.S.

A TPS holder who has been continuously present in the U.S. for more than two years has a right to an immigration hearing before removal, where they may be able to apply for asylum or other relief. Others may hope to switch to a different status, but most TPS holders cannot obtain a student or employment visa. Some would have to apply from outside the U.S., some face years of quota backlogs, and some are from countries under a travel ban.

Past immigration violations or insufficient financial resources would also disqualify them. Most significantly, TPS holders are unlikely to convince an immigration officer that they intend to return home after their visa’s purpose is complete, as most visas require – especially someone from a country in distress due to violence or environmental disaster, the reason they have TPS in the first place.

Some 300,000 people from El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine and Lebanon are set to lose status this year. Ukraine and Lebanon are in active war, so terminating TPS means deporting those people to war zones, which is what TPS was meant to prevent. Some TPS holders from El Salvador and Sudan have lived in the U.S. for more than 20 years.

Perhaps the 1990 Congress did not anticipate that individuals with TPS would make the U.S. their home for so long. Whatever it envisioned, it did not limit TPS to a fixed time. In my analysis, Percival’s assertion that TPS was always meant to be temporary is not, by itself, an “appropriate” reason to end protection.

text:
Reporters Committee attorneys are representing independent journalist Jackie Botts in a new Freedom of Information Act lawsuit seeking access to records that could help shine a light on a deadly immigration raid at a California cannabis farm last year.

In a complaint filed on Thursday in federal district court, Reporters Committee attorneys argue that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and 10 other federal agencies violated FOIA by failing to provide Botts with records she requested about the raid at Glass House Farms, which resulted in hundreds of arrests and the death of a 56-year-old farm worker.

Botts’s requests sought a range of records, including warrants, police body-worn camera footage, and use-of-force reports. As Botts reported for The Guardian in August, “the Glass House raids epitomized the high-profile, violent tactics that defined the first year of Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.”

“Getting these records is crucial to understanding how these massive, militarized — and ultimately deadly — immigration raids unfolded and why so many details of the event remain shielded from public view,” Botts said. “The public — and the families ripped apart by the raids — deserve to know.”

The lawsuit is the Reporters Committee’s latest effort to help the public better understand the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration crackdown across the United States.

Last year, Reporters Committee published a new guide, available in English and Spanish, to help journalists understand legal issues they may encounter while reporting on immigration enforcement and deportation. Reporters Committee attorneys have represented journalists in lawsuits against state and federal governments to obtain immigration enforcement records, fought to lift access restrictions related to immigration proceedings, and advocated for press rights during immigration-related coverage.

Last month alone, for example, Reporters Committee attorneys filed two new lawsuits on behalf of news outlets in Pennsylvania and Louisiana challenging secrecy surrounding how state governments are working with federal immigration enforcement agencies. Reporters Committee attorneys representing Oklahoma newsrooms filed a similar lawsuit in that state in May.

And in February, a FOIA lawsuit that Reporters Committee attorneys brought on behalf of The Guardian shook loose data that revealed the vast majority of people who were targeted for deportation for the first time in 2025 had no criminal history.

“The public has a right to know how its government is carrying out an unprecedented immigration enforcement campaign,” said Reporters Committee Staff Attorney Gunita Singh. “Too often, journalists covering these enforcement actions and its impact on their communities face legal obstacles designed to keep the public in the dark. We’re committed to helping shine a light.”

title: ICE bans hugging inside California's largest detention center. Families are fighting back
description:

A photo of the visitation area published by the state DoJ showed there was space for contact visits.
During a visit in July, Lee’s group ran into the California City warden, Christopher Chestnut, the reverend recalled.
‘Mom can have a voice’ In the face of long-term detention without contact visits, California City residents began organizing.
Some residents had advocates film them on video calls pleading for contact visits, which were published on social media.
text:
Teresa Reyes drove 300 miles to be with her son on his 32nd birthday in May, but she couldn’t give him a gift, share a meal with him or give him a hug. She couldn’t even touch him.

Her son, Guillermo, a tattoo artist from San Jose, is locked up in the California City immigration detention center, California’s largest Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility, and the only way he can see his mother is behind a thick pane of glass.

The detention center, housing roughly 1,600 people in a desert region north of Los Angeles, has denied contact visits to all people held inside since the Trump administration opened the site one year ago. That means no one inside the facility, which is run by private prison firm CoreCivic, can sit with or embrace family members who travel to the remote site for visits. Instead, families are left talking through phones while their relatives sit in an adjacent room, separated by glass barriers.

“I want to hold my son, I want to touch him, I want to assure him everything is going to be OK, but I can’t,” said Reyes, 63, speaking in Spanish. “When I see him, I have to hold back tears. I have to pretend to be strong, because I don’t want him to think I am suffering.”

The total denial of contact visits is an extreme restriction for any prison or detention site where people are locked up long-term, particularly a facility holding people accused of immigration violations. Prisons across the US housing people convicted of serious criminal offenses typically operate visitation rooms where families can sit at tables, only temporarily barring contact visits when there are safety concerns.

The harsh policy, advocates say, is part of the Trump administration’s strategy of placing more and more people in crowded facilities while their cases drag on, subjecting them to prison-like conditions and restricting their connections to the outside – all which can increase pressure to accept deportations.

In California City, detained residents aren’t staying quiet, instead working with advocates to launch a public campaign, pleading with their warden to let them hug their relatives. Is he listening?

Six months of ‘isolation’

Allen Tayson, 37, spoke over the loud clangs and shouts behind him. The father of two from Gilroy, a California city south of San Jose, was appearing on a video call from inside the California City facility, his face going in and out of focus, with the ICE messaging app blurring the background behind him.

“We feel isolated in here,” he said. “Everything is meant to break you down and discourage you and make you give up hope. If I was able to hug and hold my wife and kids, it would be like a brief getaway that would take me away from this setting. I’d cherish every second.”

Tayson, a repair shop worker, hasn’t been able to hold his family since February when he was detained by ICE at his green card interview at a United States Citizenship and Immigration Services office.

Tayson is from the Philippines and came to the US as a child. He and his wife, Samantha Sanchez, a US citizen, have known each other since they were teenagers and married in 2016. They have a 14-year-old son and five-year-old daughter – and Sanchez is now seven months pregnant. Tayson has missed nearly her entire pregnancy.

“I’m so used to taking care of my family, and I feel so helpless every single day that I’m here and my family has to figure out a way to get by without me,” said Tayson.

When Tayson arrived at California City and learned contact visits were banned for all, he and his wife made a choice: she would not travel 300 miles to visit if they couldn’t have contact. They knew first-hand how painful that process could be. When their son was around three years old, Tayson had a stint in a jail for firearm felony charges that were later dismissed. That facility only allowed visits behind glass, and at the end of one visit, his son reached out to hug his father and collided with the glass. Tayson is haunted by his son’s look of disbelief and vowed that would never happen again.

So the family talks on video calls, which cost 21 cents a minute, or $6.30 for half an hour, a cost that adds up as Sanchez works to provide for her two kids – all while navigating a high-risk pregnancy.

“I have this baby growing inside me, and he hasn’t even touched my belly,” Sanchez said. She wants to see her husband in the flesh so she has some reassurances that he is physically OK. She is trying to manage her stress and depression, worried her declining mental health will lead to pregnancy complications: “It would just be a bit of relief on my nervous system to hug him.”

Their five-year-old daughter asks daily when her father is coming home, Sanchez said. She often catches her daughter praying alone. “She says, ‘I’m just talking to God, so he can help dad.’”

A nationwide problem

The lack of access to visitation is a growing human rights crisis across the US, advocates say. Of the 10 ICE detention centers with the largest populations, four entirely bar contact visits – California City, the Stewart detention center in Georgia, the South Texas processing center in Pearsall and the Montgomery processing center in Conroe, Texas, according to ICE’s websites.

Michelle Brané, a former immigration detention ombudsman for the Department of Homeland Security, said before 2016, it was common for ICE facilities to offer contact visits. But in Trump’s first term, more detention centers began only offering visits behind glass – and it has been a persistent problem since.

Some detention centers, including Otay Mesa in San Diego, have at times had particularly restrictive set-ups, with families arriving at the facilities to discover the visit involves them video conferencing with their loved one in another room, often with a poor connection, said Brané.

Brané, now executive director of advocacy group Together and Free, said detention officials have often claimed there wasn’t enough space in the facilities to accommodate contact visits. That explanation rings hollow for the current administration, which has allotted record funds for detention, she said. “When you have as much money as this administration, there’s no excuse for inhumane conditions.”

After auditing California City in the spring, the California department of justice said the prohibition on contact visits appeared to violate a CoreCivic policy that the company provided to the state, which stipulated that there should be opportunities for physical contact and those visits should only be restricted for “security risks”.

A photo of the visitation area published by the state DoJ showed there was space for contact visits. The room has picnic tables, which families used years prior when the facility was a state prison. But now, ICE detainees aren’t allowed to sit at those tables or enter that part of the room. Instead, the photo showed, there is a row of windows at the edge of the room where the detained immigrants can speak through phones – the only available option for visits.

The Rev Deborah Lee, executive director of the Interfaith Movement for Human Integrity, a group supporting detainees, said some visitors have struggled to hear through the phones that families and detainees have to use to talk to one another. Because only one person can speak through the phone at a time, group conversations weren’t possible. “It’s just a denial of people’s humanity,” Lee said.

During a visit in July, Lee’s group ran into the California City warden, Christopher Chestnut, the reverend recalled. When she asked him why no one could have a regular visit, he told her that facilities with contact visits had higher overdose rates, without providing further explanation, according to Lee.

ICE did not respond to requests for comment. Ryan Gustin, a CoreCivic spokesperson, defended California City’s policies, saying in an email: “Facility leadership, in conjunction with our government partners, has determined that non-contact visitation is the most appropriate approach given security considerations. As with correctional and detention facilities across the country, preventing the introduction of contraband is a significant safety and security concern.”

Gustin added that CoreCivic “recognizes the importance of maintaining family and community connections for individuals in our care” and that under “applicable detention standards”, individual facilities have the authority to set visitation policies based on “factors including facility design, operational requirements, staffing considerations and security protocols”. ICE and CoreCivic did not respond to interview requests for the warden.

‘Mom can have a voice’

In the face of long-term detention without contact visits, California City residents began organizing. In April, Gustavo Guevara, who had been detained at the facility since it opened in August 2025, helped organize a letter within his dorm demanding officials offer regular visits.

He said the idea spread to other dorms, with residents writing their own demand letters. Some residents had come from other ICE facilities where contact visits were allowed, so were bewildered and angry to lose that access. People were especially anxious about never getting to say goodbye to relatives if they lost their cases.

“Not only are you immediately deprived of that human interaction, but what is hanging over your head is the possibility of being sent to another country, not knowing if you’ll ever hold your loved ones again,” he said.

Guevara and others worked with the California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice (CCIJ), an Oakland-based nonprofit that advocates for detained people, and a coalition of activists delivered the letters to the warden and helped launch a “Hugs Beyond Bars” campaign.

Some residents had advocates film them on video calls pleading for contact visits, which were published on social media. Allen Tayson also recorded himself reading his own demand letter, which the coalition released on Instagram.

“Across all the dorms, people could unite behind this,” said Val Suarez, CCIJ community and legal organizer. “They saw this big family room that used to be a visitation room which proves there really is no reason for them to not have access to this.” It felt achievable.

It was personal for Guevara, who had a close friend visit him regularly at California City behind glass. That was until June when he was deported to Mexico. Guevara never got to hug him and doesn’t know if he’ll see him again, he said, but he’ll continue advocating for contact visits for those he left behind.

Last month, Samantha Sanchez also joined CCIJ for a visit to US senator Alex Padilla’s office in San Francisco urging Congress to pressure CoreCivic to provide visitation. “I wanted my kids to see that mom can have a voice – that I’m doing this for dad and other families,” Sanchez said.

The senator’s office seemed sympathetic to their pleas, advocates said. But so far, CoreCivic and the California City warden have not responded to their demands.

During Teresa Reyes’s visit with her son in May on his birthday, she noticed there were vending machines for visitors and hoped to buy a snack for her son, but learned that was not possible.

When advocates accompanying her asked if the staff could make an exception and give her one brief hug, the officers said no, she recalled.

She hasn’t been back to California City since May – and will only return if she can hug her son.

CHICAGO (WLS) -- A Chicago Public Schools custodian who was detained by federal immigration authorities at a routine immigration hearing has been released from ICE custody and reunited with his family after 42 days in detention.

Josue Pire-Hidalgo returned to Chicago and spoke exclusively with the ABC7 I-Team about his time in custody.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

"Every day felt like an eternity for me being in there. Conditions are not the best ,so it was very difficult for me to withstand detention under those conditions for that long," Pire-Hidalgo said through an attorney translating his remarks.

His wife, Yulexis Padilla Julio, was also detained in front of their children but was later released with an ankle monitor. While her husband remained in custody, she advocated for his release.

"Very conflicting feelings because here we are trying and we were doing things well we were following the process and so we were not expecting this to happen to us to him," Padilla Julio said.

Pire-Hidalgo said returning to everyday family life has been meaningful since his release.

"It was marvelous to be with my family again after being detained there for 42 days, just seeing them and spending time with them was incredible," he said.

SEE ALSO | ICE plans to use robot dogs, electrified gloves, social media tracking for immigration enforcement

Carla Espinoza, an immigration attorney with EZG Immigration Law and a former Chicago immigration judge, said Pire-Hidalgo is originally from Venezuela. She said he works as a custodian at Farnsworth Elementary School, has no criminal record, holds temporary protected status and has a pending asylum application.

Despite those circumstances, Espinoza said, he was arrested by federal authorities at a routine immigration hearing.

When asked what justified the detention, Espinoza responded: "None. And I think that's what we're seeing, just a policy of detention, regardless of the circumstances of that particular individual."

Espinoza said immigration enforcement tactics have shifted, with authorities increasingly detaining non-citizens as they attend immigration check-ins and comply with legal requirements. She said those efforts are occurring alongside more targeted street enforcement operations, rather than the larger-scale enforcement campaigns seen in Chicago and elsewhere last year.

According to the Department of Homeland Security, immigration authorities made a record 51,000 arrests last month. An I-Team analysis of federal data found that nearly half the people arrested in Illinois since the start of President Donald Trump's second term had no criminal charges.

The same I-Team analysis found that 72% of people detained by ICE in Illinois have been deported since the start of the president's second term.

The Department of Homeland Security has maintained that its enforcement efforts are focused on what it describes as the "worst of the worst."
